Part 2 Boundaries and Methods ​

The ultimate object domain of this framework is the broadly conceived empirical structural world. Natural processes, technical systems, ecological processes, human actions, organizations, and institutions can all enter structural explanation if they can leave comparable materials and allow researchers to declare candidate objects, states, relations or transitions, interfaces, time windows, scale profiles, and identity criteria. The human structured world is not a synonym for the world as a whole. It is a specialized domain within that world, requiring additional human-domain clauses, normative commitments, and authorization procedures. Purely metaphysical assertions, objects for which no empirical fields can be supplied, and “systems” established solely through naming or narrative coherence do not enter empirical judgment. They may be discussed, but they must not borrow this framework's levels of empirical conclusions.

The current scope of application must still be declared separately each time: the object, SP/T/K, region or environment, data window, extrapolation unit, and exclusions. Belonging to the broadly conceived empirical structural world means only that a contract[1] can in principle be established. It does not imply that any conclusion can be directly generalized across windows, objects, or domains.

This choice of scope also sets the framework's limits. The framework seeks to explain how objects form identifiable structures, how they operate, how they change or undergo dissolution under the effects of conditions, and how descriptions at different scales can be converted. It does not presuppose a unified purpose for the world, project human intentions onto nonhuman processes, or infer “how one should choose” directly from “what is.” Real-world choices are taken up by the normative layer and operational procedures separately.

02Note

Understanding this section

Part 2 Boundaries and Methods

Whether something may enter discussion, what kind of support it can receive, and whether action may be based on it are three different questions. Part 2 first defines the theory's scope of use, then explains what evidence each kind of conclusion requires.

Broadly conceived concerns the variety of objects: natural processes, technology, ecology, human action, and institutions may all be candidates. Empirical narrows admission: comparable materials must exist, and the object, states, relations or transitions, interfaces, time, scale, and identity must be made clear. This does not claim that a single mechanism already explains all these domains, still less prove that the world necessarily has a common purpose.

The human structured world is one class of these objects. Discussing people requires additional roles, culture, norms, and authorization. Human purposes must not be assigned to wind, water, algorithms, or ecological processes. Equally, the fact that an object concerns people does not make factual judgments inherently carry authority to act on them. Part 1's general outline is recast here as working boundaries; the later H, N, and O respectively take up domain adaptation, value premises, and operational procedures.

Each application must state its current contract anew: what the object is, which scale profile SP represents, which period T covers, and on what basis K identifies the earlier and later object as the same. Then specify environment, region, data window, extrapolation unit, and exclusions. The broad overall object domain does not replace this narrow contract. Modeling a queue in one window, for example, does not explain every queue or permit directly transplanting its treatment into another institutional setting.

Purely metaphysical propositions may be discussed as philosophical questions, but without comparable materials and empirical fields they cannot borrow this book's evidential levels for empirical judgments. This restriction concerns the status of the conclusion; it does not declare the question meaningless. Conversely, empirical fields merely allow a testable question to be posed. Specific support must still be established through subsequent instances.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: empirical judgments require comparable materials and clear referents; otherwise, different observations cannot establish what is being compared.

  2. 2

    Connection: a broad object domain cannot eliminate differences in environment, time, and measurement, so the overall scope must be narrowed to the current contract on each occasion.

  3. 3

    Conclusion: structural explanation may be conducted across many kinds of object, but each conclusion holds only within a scope supported by materials and bridges.

  4. 4

    Responsibility: description and explanation rest on materials and inference. Who should be protected and who may act additionally require disclosed normative premises and authorization; they cannot be inferred from the object's being open to study.

Distinctions to keep clear

Object domain

Which kinds of object may in principle be studied.

≠

Scope of the present application

The objects, time, scale, environment, and exclusions actually studied on this occasion.

Explaining an object

Explains how it forms, operates, undergoes conversion, or dissolves.

≠

Assigning an object a purpose

Claims that it pursues a goal; this requires support from its object type and materials.

Teaching construction: a scope contract for one conveyor beltTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll equipment and periods are illustrative; no actual observational data are included.

Suppose the study covers only one conveyor segment during a factory's day shift. B is its entrance and exit, X its belt speed and number of queued items, R the arrival and departure rules, I the upstream and downstream interfaces, and T one shift. SP is a nine-axis profile: abbreviated here, A aggregation level is this equipment segment, X spatial extent runs from the specified entrance to exit, T time span is one shift, and R resolution is the registered sampling protocol for belt speed and the queue. K requires the equipment and interfaces to retain specified relations. The five axes not developed—O organization, C causation, I influence, N network, and J jurisdiction and authorization—are omitted only in this teaching example. A complete application must still register each axis's status, with reasons where genuinely inapplicable. SP must not be reduced to resolution alone. The example specifies which process segment is being asked about. If the product or interfaces change on the night shift, the old contract does not automatically cover it.

BoundaryThe example only shows what the fields are for. It neither establishes explanatory gain from this grouping nor authorizes changes to production.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: naming all things that go badly as a system without common states, a window, or comparable materials.

What it limitsA name cannot produce a testable empirical object. It may remain a narrative question, but must not be assigned a level of empirical support.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • A system without empirical fields cannot receive the standing of an empirical conclusion; nor does naming an observable object automatically confer formal G support.
  • Narrowing the scope of application generally corrects extrapolation; it does not withdraw all supported local facts.
  • Selection in natural processes, outputs of technical systems, and human intentions must not be equated merely because the same word for choice or selection appears.

Scope and open questions

This introduction defines the object domain and scope of use; the teaching contract directly illustrates its logic. Additional historical facts cannot validate that choice of scope, so an actual case is not forced into the discussion.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    A conclusion comes from one term at one school. A researcher says, “Schools all belong to the human structured world, so it applies to every school.” What is missing?

  2. 2

    If a mathematical model explains the outcome of resource allocation, has it already answered what distribution would be justified?

A conclusion comes from one term at one school. A researcher says, “Schools all belong to the human structured world, so it applies to every school.” What is missing?

What is missing is a basis for bridging and extrapolation across objects, periods, and environments. Membership in one overall object domain merely permits study; it does not guarantee the same mechanism or effect.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a mathematical model explains the outcome of resource allocation, has it already answered what distribution would be justified?

No. The model may explain the results of given rules. Justification requires explicit value premises, benefits and risks, the decision-maker, and authorization procedures.

2.1Two-Stage Object Admission ​

In briefFirst state the question clearly, then test it. Registering a candidate is like specifying the address of a research question; formal support depends on comparisons and results agreed beforehand. These two steps must not be reversed.
Codes used in this section (3)
  • D0Structural Object
  • G1Conditional Gain from Candidate Grouping
  • G4Representational Closure and Object or Intervention Conversion

Structural modeling begins with candidate objects, without presupposing that the grouping has already received support for a grouping gain, and without letting a declaration substitute for grounds for object facts. When applying for formal support for root instances within this framework, object admission has two stages whose order must not be reversed. This procedure governs strong empirical claims made under G and the C and CM claims that depend on it. It is not a universal truth check for all domain knowledge, historical records, or everyday understanding.

The first stage is the declaration of a candidate object. The analyst registers S*=<B,X,R,I,T,SP,K> under a D0 contract: boundary B, state variables X, relations or transition constraints R, interface I, time window T, scale profile SP, and identity criterion K. The asterisk indicates that the object remains an analytical candidate. Complete fields establish only that the question has been stated clearly. They do not establish that the grouping has relatively independent empirical standing in the world. When fields are incomplete, only exploratory questions may be proposed.

The second stage is testing of root instances. When the analyst claims grouping gains, effects of specified channels, historical conditional increments, or scale closure under G1–G4, and applies for eligibility for formal support within this framework, a corresponding G-instance must be established. Before viewing the results, an immutable contract version and an auditable timestamp must be used to freeze the null model N0, a single subtype, one success criterion selected from that subtype's admissible list, controls, models, samples and extrapolation units, evaluation metrics, positive thresholds, decision rules, rules for null conclusions, falsification conditions, and suspension conditions. Instances with multiple targets or models must also freeze the primary target or aggregation, model selection or ensembling, and rules for multiple comparisons. This support eligibility belongs to the specific instance that passes the test, not to the D0 declaration or the abstract templates G1–G4.

Support eligibility requires that exploratory work be kept separate from confirmatory work, positive results from null conclusions, and completed freezing from post hoc deviations. Only confirmatory or replication instances completed under a contract frozen before the evidence can provide positive support. Falsification instances support only the pre-registered falsification or null-model judgment. Exploratory work, drafts, post-evidence deviations, or undisclosed deviations can only generate candidates, register deviations, or remain unresolved. They must not use formal-instance eligibility to support C branches that require that eligibility. Failure to pass the positive-support check does not automatically support N0 either. Unless equivalence or sufficiency, statistical power or sensitivity, and tolerance have been pre-registered and their requirements met, the conclusion can only be “not positively supported” or “unresolved.” Thus, “the candidate object has been registered,” “positive G is not supported,” “the null model is supported,” and “the instance receives limited positive support” must remain distinct states.

This two-stage structure prevents two opposite errors: treating the analyst's naming, clustering, or boundary choice as meaning that a grouping gain or object facts have already been supported; and piecing scattered materials together after the fact into an unfalsifiable “system” before the object has even been declared.

2.1Note

Understanding this section

2.1 Two-Stage Object Admission

First state the question clearly, then test it. Registering a candidate is like specifying the address of a research question; formal support depends on comparisons and results agreed beforehand. These two steps must not be reversed.

In D0, S*=〈B,X,R,I,T,SP,K〉lists, in order, boundaries, state variables, relations or transition constraints, interfaces, time window, scale profile, and identity criterion. The asterisk reminds readers that it is a candidate. Completing every field does not establish an optimal boundary, relative independence of the object, or the existence of a mechanism. Exploration remains possible when essential fields are missing, but the contract must not be falsely presented as clear.

The second stage governs only claims seeking formal G1–G4 instance support and strong empirical C and CM claims that depend on such support. G1 asks about grouping gain, G2 about specified channels, G3 about historical conditional increments relative to the current representation, and G4 about representational closure and conversion. G3 in particular does not ask the general question of whether history ever influenced the present. Researchers must select the corresponding question rather than use one class of results to endorse another.

Before viewing the results, freeze an immutable version with an auditable timestamp: N0, a unique subtype, the single success criterion permitted for that subtype, controls and models, sample and extrapolation units, indicators, positive thresholds, decision and null-conclusion rules, and falsification and suspension conditions. Multiple targets or models also require freezing the primary target or aggregation rule, model selection or ensembling, and multiple-comparison rules. Freezing is intended not to make the world obey a form, but to prevent moving the question and success threshold after seeing the results.

A confirmatory or replication instance gains eligibility for the corresponding positive support only after completing and passing checks under its advance contract. A falsification instance supports only the falsification or null judgment originally registered. Exploration, drafts, deviations after evidence, and undisclosed deviations must not enter C branches requiring formal support through a formal-support edge. Deviations may be honestly recorded and a new proposal made, but the exploratory history must not be erased.

Retain at least four statuses: registered candidate; not positively supported; the null model is supported; and grouping gain receives limited positive support. Failure to pass the positive rule may reflect a small effect, inadequate measurement, insufficient sample size, or an unsuitable model; it does not automatically mean absence. Supporting equivalence or sufficiency within a specified tolerance additionally requires advance null-conclusion rules and statistical power or sensitivity, with the corresponding criteria met. §2.1.1 preserves what was already grounded in earlier research; §2.1.2 prevents formal proof from being treated as real-world samples.

v2 expressly limits the second-stage result to grouping gain. Registering an object, supporting object facts with reliable material, and obtaining G1 support for grouping gain within a task are three different things. A reliable membership record may support facts about a team and its members, without showing that grouping by this team predicts outcomes better than a matched ungrouped N0.

For example, an institution established by law cannot have its legal standing or membership denied merely because it has never undergone G1 testing. Conversely, accurate prediction from statistical grouping does not establish a unified will. Settle specific standing under constitutive conditions, predictive advantage under G1, and causal effects through the relevant channels separately.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First premise: analysts may initially choose boundaries and representations, but the choice itself is not evidence that the choice has empirical standing.

  2. 2

    Second premise: if comparison methods, thresholds, or models change with results already seen, a positive result may arise from retrospective selection and cannot be interpreted under the original contract.

  3. 3

    Connection: first define a candidate through D0, then fix the testing contract for the requested G subtype before the evidence, making both the question and the decision procedure reviewable.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: eligibility attaches to specific instances satisfying the contract, not to blank templates or to every completely filled-out candidate.

  5. 5

    Responsibility for null judgments: not rejecting N0 is not equivalent to supporting N0 in a prespecified sense. Equivalence/sufficiency, tolerance, and identification sensitivity must each satisfy their requirements.

Distinctions to keep clear

D0 completed

The question about the object can be described.

≠

G-instance support

A specific empirical question frozen beforehand receives limited support.

Not positively supported

The positive rule was not passed; the issue may remain unresolved.

≠

Null-model support

Meaningful departures have been excluded under the prespecified null rule.

Truth or falsity of an empirical effect

Whether the difference being asked about exists in the world.

≠

Eligibility for formal support

Whether the current information and research procedure suffice to provide the specified support under this framework.

Teaching construction: registering a queue does not prove that grouping is usefulTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe comparison concerns G1-style grouping gain, not the effect of a causal intervention. Actual information is required to form a formal instance.

Suppose researchers want to know whether grouping service requests by interface predicts waiting time more accurately than not grouping them. First register B, X, R, I, T, SP, and K; then fix the baseline, error measure, minimum improvement, and evaluation rules before an independent evaluation window. If grouping is changed after evaluation results are seen, the resulting pattern may be a new candidate, but must not masquerade as confirmation frozen beforehand. No study has been carried out here, and no numerical improvement has been invented.

BoundaryThis is a teaching example of the procedure. It does not claim to have passed G1 or infer improved service quality from a complete candidate.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching conditional counterexample: after only two very noisy measurements fail to reach a positive threshold, someone announces that the effect is zero.

What it limitsWithout an advance null rule and sensitivity, the result is at most not positively supported. Failure with a small sample does not automatically exclude meaningful differences.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleTeaching conditional counterexample: a researcher uses the same evaluation results to choose one of the ten best groupings, then describes it as the “sole preregistered model.”

What it limitsThis violates freezing before evidence. Its honest status is exploration with a record of deviations, not confirmatory support.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • This procedure is not a universal truth check for all domain knowledge, historical records, and ordinary understanding. Existing research must not be invalidated wholesale for lacking G contracts.
  • An arbitrarily drawn threshold does not become scientific by being a threshold. Measurement validity, sample selection, competing explanations, and extrapolation conditions still require separate support.
  • Repeatedly adjusting a model on the same data does not turn it into independent confirmation. Retain its exploratory status before designing a genuinely new test.

Scope and open questions

This section concerns procedural conditions for formal support. A construction can clearly show differences in status; actual historical material is placed in the next section to test the boundary of “old evidence status.” This section does not fabricate a real preregistration example.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    A set of results fails to reach the positive threshold, but no equivalence tolerance was preregistered. Should its status be recorded as the null model is established?

  2. 2

    After registering a complete D0, may one immediately state that the system has objective independent standing?

  3. 3

    If the same information has already helped select a model, does subsequently locking the file count as freezing before results?

A set of results fails to reach the positive threshold, but no equivalence tolerance was preregistered. Should its status be recorded as the null model is established?

No. It may be recorded as not positively supported or unresolved; a zero conclusion requires additional rules and sufficient sensitivity.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

After registering a complete D0, may one immediately state that the system has objective independent standing?

No. D0 fixes only what the candidate refers to; relative independence, grouping gain, and other empirical claims require corresponding comparisons and evidence.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If the same information has already helped select a model, does subsequently locking the file count as freezing before results?

Not for material already used to select the model. Disclose exposure to the material and its exploratory use, and freeze a new contract when suitable new confirmatory material is used.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

2.1.1Domain Evidence and Formal Instance Eligibility ​

In briefEarlier research can be valuable while lacking eligibility as a formal instance of this framework. Preserve what it originally established; if stronger standing is sought, add a genuinely new test.

Existing studies, archives, oral accounts, archaeological materials, and locatable source texts can support the relevant descriptions, explanations, or limited causal conclusions according to their actual research designs. When these materials are used, whether they are pre-registered confirmatory work, post hoc findings, exploratory work, historical reconstruction, or other research should be preserved accurately. A pre-result contract must not be fabricated for them. These materials cannot thereby acquire G-instance support automatically, nor do they lose their originally supported content merely because they have not yet been converted into G-instance form.

If an existing finding is to be used in a new formal root instance, it may first serve as a source of questions and models, then be tested using independent materials, a later window, or an appropriate replication design. Data used for exploratory work must be separated from data used for confirmatory work, and model selection from final evaluation. Where no feasible new test is available, retain the domain conclusion and the relation awaiting testing; do not fabricate confirmation.

Formal proofs hold under their axioms, semantics, and rules of derivation. Textual interpretation is open to criticism on the basis of editions, contexts, and argumentative materials. Normative claims disclose their value premises and reasons. They can contribute to analysis, but must not masquerade as one another's empirical mechanisms, factual truth, or real-world authorization.

2.1.1Note

Understanding this section

2.1.1 Domain evidence and eligibility as a formal instance

Earlier research can be valuable while lacking eligibility as a formal instance of this framework. Preserve what it originally established; if stronger standing is sought, add a genuinely new test.

This section prevents two opposite misuses. One rewrites past exploration or historical reconstruction as preregistered confirmation. The other discards all locatable historical material and research conclusions because today's forms did not exist then. The source permits retaining descriptions, explanations, or bounded causal conclusions actually supported by the research design, while prohibiting fabrication of a pre-outcome contract.

“Existing finding → source of a new question/model → new contract → test with new material” is a viable continuation. Independent material, a later time window, or appropriate replication may offer a new evaluation opportunity, but independence must be explained: one cannot tune a model using all the data and then relabel part of it as a previously unseen validation set. A later window still requires checking changes in objects and measurements.

If no feasible new test exists, state the existing domain conclusions and relations awaiting testing, rather than forcing them into a G-instance. Formal proof, textual interpretation, and normative argument can also contribute, using their respective grounds: axioms and derivations, versions and context, and value premises and reasons. They supply one another with questions and constraints, without impersonating real mechanisms or authorization.

This section uses Snow's case solely to examine the coexistence of historical material and current eligibility. The field investigation, interviews, and limitations in the 1855 text are historical evidence open to criticism; they do not lose their content because a contemporary G contract is absent. Nor have we used them to reconstruct a nonexistent pre-outcome timestamp.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: the way existing material was produced is already historical; its pre-event or post-event status cannot be retrospectively changed today.

  2. 2

    Connection: evaluating the scope of evidence and evaluating eligibility under a particular framework are separate questions, so they can be recorded separately without canceling each other.

  3. 3

    Conclusion one: preserve domain content actually supported by the design while stating that it has not automatically obtained positive support as a G-instance.

  4. 4

    Conclusion two: if new eligibility is sought, first freeze a new question and evaluate it with suitable new material; if no feasible new test exists, retain the domain conclusion and its pending-test status.

  5. 5

    Responsibilities: sources supply historical facts and research design; the present explanation supplies the mapping and the inference ceiling. Normative claims and authorization have separate grounds.

Distinctions to keep clear

Domain evidence

Supports bounded conclusions under the original research design.

≠

Formal G eligibility

The standing of a specific instance obtained under this framework's pre-evidence contract.

Reinterpreting old material

Can propose different models and questions.

≠

Fabricating past preregistration

Disguises a retrospective finding as a pre-outcome commitment, changing the status of the material.

Independent analysis

Another algorithm may reveal implementation problems.

≠

Independent confirmatory material

Its evaluation has not already been used by the same model-selection process; its provenance and dependencies must still be stated.

Broad Street, London, 1854: preserve the evidence and the differences between questionsDocumented case

In the second edition of 1855, Snow reported consulting death registers and investigating drinking-water habits; he presented the circumstances to the parish on September 7, 1854, and the pump handle was removed the next day. The original also states that incidence had already fallen substantially before use of the well water ceased, so it could not establish whether the water still had a disease-causing effect at that time. Here we preserve the distinction between “what the investigation reported” and “whether the net intervention effect was identified.”

SourceJohn Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855, 2nd ed.Printed pages 39–41 and 51–52; the passages The Cholera near Golden Square and The Pump-well in Broad StreetReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is the author's historical account of his investigation at the time, not this lesson's revalidation of every cause of the disease. The material can support a bounded exposure explanation; temporal sequence alone cannot estimate the effect of removing the handle, nor constitute a modern G preregistration.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceSnow himself noted that incidence had already fallen markedly before use of the well water ceased, and stated that it was impossible to determine whether active disease-causing matter remained in the well when it was closed.

What it limitsThis limits the narrative that “removing the handle caused the entire decline,” but does not also invalidate his investigation of water exposure.

John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera

What does not follow

  • Snow's material on water exposure and the effect of removing the pump handle concern two different causal questions. Support for the former does not mean the latter has been separately identified.
  • Historical evidence need not become a G-instance to be discussed; likewise, being “historically famous” does not exempt a particular causal narrative from criticism.
  • This lesson did not recheck the original death registers or obtain individual-level data. The case relies on relevant passages in Snow's original work, rather than repeating a historical epidemiological study.

Scope and open questions

Historical material with explicit dates, provenance, and acknowledged limitations can directly show that domain evidence and eligibility under a new framework do not cancel each other.

  • Reestimating the net effect of removing the handle using a modern comparative design would require fuller material on exposure, departures, onset times, and comparable counterfactuals; this lesson does not have that material.

  2. 2

    If a researcher cannot obtain any new material, must earlier findings be rejected?

  3. 3

    Can “the fall in incidence after removal of the pump handle” be taken directly as the net effect of removing it?

Can an investigation from 1855 without a G-instance record still serve as material for the historical question of water exposure?

Yes, according to its investigative design, account, and limitations; do not fabricate a G preregistration for that time or automatically award formal support under this framework.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a researcher cannot obtain any new material, must earlier findings be rejected?

No. Retain originally supported domain conclusions and explain that the new formal eligibility has not been established.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can “the fall in incidence after removal of the pump handle” be taken directly as the net effect of removing it?

No. A counterfactual comparison is needed, addressing competing explanations such as the decline having already begun, population departure, and limitations of the material.

2.1.2Connecting Formal Conclusions and Empirical Instances ​

In briefMathematics can rigorously answer “does this hold under these assumptions?” Real-world application must also answer “does this object satisfy these assumptions?” One answer may be determinate while the other remains unresolved.

Formal propositions first specify the state domain, mapping, target, admissible operations, and logical premises; proof then establishes their conclusions. Exhaustive enumeration of a complete finite domain can test every case within that domain. Numerical computation must also specify precision, boundary determination, and implementation error. Proof, exhaustive enumeration, and numerical checks can cross-check one another, but together they do not generate real-world samples, and more computations do not increase independent empirical support.

Applying a formal conclusion to a real-world object requires a separate account of how real-world quantities correspond to model variables, which premises are already supported by materials, whether the errors and applicable ranges are acceptable, and what counterexamples would invalidate the mapping. “The proposition holds in the given model” and “whether the real-world object satisfies the model remains undetermined” can both be acknowledged. A mathematical counterexample is already sufficient to refute the unconditional inference it addresses. The absence of a completed real-world experiment does not erase this formal answer. Conversely, formal feasibility, the existence of an algorithm, computability within budget, timely availability of data, correct execution in practice, and authority to adopt are six judgments, each requiring its own basis.

2.1.2Note

Understanding this section

2.1.2 Connecting formal conclusions with empirical instances

Mathematics can rigorously answer “does this hold under these assumptions?” Real-world application must also answer “does this object satisfy these assumptions?” One answer may be determinate while the other remains unresolved.

A formal proposition first fixes the state domain, mapping, target, permitted operations, and logical premises. A proof explains how the conclusion follows from those premises; exhaustive checking over a finite domain checks every declared case; numerical checking must additionally specify precision, boundaries, and implementation error. These three can cross-check errors, but computation does not generate new real-world samples.

Connection to reality must be established item by item: what observable quantities the model variables correspond to; whether measurement and representation preserve distinctions needed for the target; which premises already have supporting material; whether error and the applicable range are acceptable; and what counterexample would overturn the mapping. The F layer in source §4.18–§4.19 particularly stresses that static recovery, dynamic closure, and intervention transferability are different propositions.

A formal counterexample suffices to refute the unconditional inference it targets. For instance, “an aggregate can always recover each component” fails with a single explicit mathematical counterexample; no factory or hospital experiment is needed first. But the counterexample does not show that every real-world aggregate is useless. If the target becomes the total, the same representation may be entirely sufficient.

Real-world adoption carries six independent responsibilities: formal feasibility; existence of an algorithm; computability within budget; timely availability of material; correct actual execution; and authority to adopt it. Passing one step does not imply passing the next. Knowing a decision rule exists may leave it both impossible to compute in time and impossible to supply with timely inputs; even computability and executability do not automatically confer authority to act upon people.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Mathematical premises: state domain X={0,1}²; representation π(x₁,x₂)=x₁+x₂; target q(x₁,x₂)=x₁; the recovery function g may read only π.

  2. 2

    Take x=(0,1) and x′=(1,0). Then π(x)=π(x′)=1, whereas q(x)=0 and q(x′)=1.

  3. 3

    If a g correct for every state existed, g(1) would have to equal both 0 and 1, a contradiction. Thus, on this complete state domain and under this representation, no single-valued function exactly recovers q.

  4. 4

    If the target changes to qΣ=x₁+x₂, then gΣ(z)=z gives exact recovery. The conclusion is target-relative; it does not say all aggregation fails.

  5. 5

    Real-world responsibility: interpreting x₁ and x₂ as real quantities requires separate support for the state domain, measurement, input availability, and permitted operations; the four-state proof supplies neither real-world occurrence frequencies nor intervention effects.

Distinctions to keep clear

Proof established

The inference is valid within the declared axioms and semantics.

≠

Real-world fit established

Sufficient material supports the variable mapping and premises for the target object.

Exhaustive checking of four states

Covers every state of this particular finite model.

≠

Four real-world observations

Material from the world, with issues of sampling, measurement, and dependence.

An algorithm exists

There is a rule for obtaining an answer.

≠

Timely, correct, and authorized execution

Computational budget, material, implementation, and permission are separately satisfied.

Mathematical construction: the same sum, two different first componentsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe domain contains only these four states; the recovery function is single-valued and reads only π, without identity labels or additional measurements.

The four states are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1); their π values are 0, 1, 1, and 2, and their q values are 0, 0, 1, and 1, respectively. The target is not constant within the group π=1, so reading only the sum cannot recover the first component. If the target becomes the sum, every representation value directly supplies the answer. This is exact integer computation over a complete finite domain.

BoundaryThis is an example of mathematical recoverability, not an estimate of real-world effects, human types, or statistical error; it cannot establish that a real system happens to satisfy the model.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleMathematical boundary: q=x₁ is not recoverable on the original four-state domain; if the admissible domain shrinks to {(0,0),(1,1)}, each value of the same π corresponds to only one state.

What it limitsRestricting the admissible domain changes the premises and therefore recoverability; failure on the original domain cannot be generalized to every restricted domain.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The mathematical counterexample already refutes “any aggregate can recover any detail,” but does not refute sufficiency when the target is the total.
  • Allowing additional information, such as x₂, changes the permitted operations and representation contract; the new recoverability cannot be counted as success under the old contract.
  • Exhaustive checking over a finite domain must list the complete domain; randomly sampling many states is still not proof over an infinite domain. Numerical near-zero does not automatically mean exact zero.

Scope and open questions

This section directly addresses formal validity and empirical connection. A complete finite mathematical construction suffices to test an unconditional inference; unrelated historical facts are not added as purported empirical evidence.

  2. 2

    In the counterexample above, can x₁ be recovered if additional access to x₂ is allowed?

  3. 3

    If a rule has been proved to exist, can one thereby declare that it can automatically go live the next day?

Does running the same four-state exhaustive check one million times add one million independent pieces of empirical support?

No. It may help reveal implementation errors, but it still checks the same model and produces no new real-world observations.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

In the counterexample above, can x₁ be recovered if additional access to x₂ is allowed?

Yes: x₁=π−x₂. But this expands the input conditions; it does not overturn the original impossibility of recovery when “only π may be read.”

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a rule has been proved to exist, can one thereby declare that it can automatically go live the next day?

No. An algorithm, budget, timely material, correct implementation, and permission to adopt it still each need support.

2.2Proposition Roles and the Burden of Argument ​

In briefA sentence such as “this system works, so it should be used” mixes at least object definition, an effect judgment, a value choice, and permission to act. Break the sentence apart first to know what each part requires as support.
Codes used in this section (10)
  • G1Conditional Gain from Candidate Grouping
  • G4Representational Closure and Object or Intervention Conversion
  • H1Meaning and Coordination
  • H4Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity
  • H5Historical Trace Carriers
  • H3Institutional Write-Back
  • H6Open-Ended Undertaking
  • F1Task Recovery
  • F5Error Propagation under Approximate Closure
  • C12Check on the Validity of Normative Bridging

Formal judgments first distinguish six commonly used roles: D, G, E, H, N, and O. Conditional formal propositions provable within a model are designated separately as F. If a single natural-language sentence mixes definitional, empirical, formal, methodological, or normative commitments, it must be separated into its components, with the basis for each stated separately. The identifiers organize the burden of argument; they do not mean that all kinds have the same truth conditions.

D, definitions. These specify how terms are used within the framework; they are not empirical facts about the world. Definitions can make judgments consistent, but cannot by themselves establish the existence of objects, mechanisms, or historical effects.

G, empirical question families. G1–G4 organize empirical questions about grouping gains, specified channels, historical conditional increments, and representational closure, respectively. Specific instances must take the form of factual assertions with an object, target, conditions, comparison, and mode of failure—for example, whether a specified difference exceeds a threshold. Whether a fact is true and whether evidence is sufficient to support it are different questions. Pre-registration, review, and release rules govern eligibility for formal support; they do not define whether an effect exists in the world.

E, epistemic constraints. These specify the valid scope of observation, measurement, inference, and cross-scale transfer, requiring that blind spots, competing explanations, and residuals be retained.

H, human-domain clauses. H1, H4, and H5 are empirical hypotheses requiring case-specific evidence. H2 is an operational classification rule. H3 is a classification rule for institutional write-back. H6 is a normative boundary. H marks adaptation to the human domain; it is not a logical type mutually exclusive with definition, empirical content, or normative content. H clauses must not be treated as an unclassified set of “axioms of human nature,” nor written back as universal roots for the nonhuman world.

N, normative commitments. These explicitly declare what the framework chooses to protect and constrain. They must not be disguised as factual propositions that empirical data could prove.

O, operational procedures. These specify the freezing of descriptions, evidence audits, normative registration, authorization, comparison of options, constrained execution, review, stopping, withdrawal, and remedy.

F, conditional formal propositions. Conclusions are established by proof under explicit state domains, mappings, targets, operation sets, and mathematical assumptions. Formal counterexamples can refute universal inferences that exceed those conditions. Whether real-world objects satisfy the premises still requires independent evidence. See §4.18 for F1–F5 and §4.19 for task families and dynamic refinement.

C is not an eighth kind of fact. It combines contracts that delimit the use of outcomes with mechanism conditions; C12 provides a bridge to normative procedures. Common method constraints govern the use of representations, evidence, and inference. They do not serve as additional laws of the world.

Descriptive conclusions cannot generate normative conclusions on their own, nor can explanation or diagnosis[2] generate authority to act on their own. The minimal bridge to real-world action is:

A descriptive or explanatory conclusion + explicit normative premises + current evidence + lawful authorization + an action ceiling + conditions for stopping or withdrawal

If any element of this bridge to real-world action is missing, real-world action should stop. The associated action requirements should remain at the level of description, candidate explanations, obtaining further evidence, non-action, or proposing a reversible probe, rather than bypassing authorization through theoretical language.

2.2Note

Understanding this section

2.2 Roles of propositions and responsibilities of argument

A sentence such as “this system works, so it should be used” mixes at least object definition, an effect judgment, a value choice, and permission to act. Break the sentence apart first to know what each part requires as support.

D answers “what does this word refer to here?” Specifying meanings for “structure” or “repair” supports consistent judgment but does not establish that the corresponding object exists in the world or has been repaired. G answers specific empirical questions: which object, which comparison, and whether a difference under which conditions exceeds a threshold. G1–G4 are families of questions; instances carry particular factual assertions. A fact may be true despite insufficient current support, and a procedurally complete inquiry may still reach a wrong conclusion through a mistaken model. Formal eligibility cannot define the world.

E constrains how much is known: measurement blind spots, competing explanations, residuals, and conditions for cross-scale transfer must be retained. N makes value choices explicit: what to protect and what to restrict. These have different responsibilities; acknowledging epistemic limits does not automatically establish a value, and choosing to protect someone does not automatically establish every description of their circumstances. O organizes freezing, auditing, normative registration, authorization, option comparison, bounded execution, review, stopping, withdrawal, and remedy into procedures. It constrains how one may proceed without replacing factual grounds.

H is especially easy to misread. It is a marker for adaptation to the human domain, not a sixth kind of truth wholly exclusive of definitions, empirical claims, and norms. H1, H4, and H5 are empirical hypotheses requiring case-specific evidence; H2 is an operational typology; H3 classifies institutional write-back; H6 is a normative boundary. Sharing the H label does not make them all a priori axioms of human nature, still less make human meaning and institutional rules the roots of all natural processes.

F consists of conditional formal propositions established by proof under explicit state domains, mappings, targets, operation sets, and mathematical premises. Mathematical counterexamples can defeat universal inferences that exceed their premises; whether reality satisfies those premises still requires evidence. F1–F5 in source §4.18 and the task families and dynamic refinements in §4.19 respectively show boundaries for recovery, dynamics, intervention, composition, and approximation; their uses cannot be treated as identical merely because they are all formulas.

C does not add another class of facts about the world alongside D and G; it supplies contracts for how results are registered and under which mechanism conditions they are used, with C12 providing the bridge to normative procedures. Common method constraints are not additional laws of the world either. Adding more numbered labels to a conclusion increases its locatability, not its independent evidence.

The minimal bridge to action contains six items: a descriptive or explanatory conclusion, explicit normative premises, current evidence, lawful authorization, an action ceiling, and stopping or withdrawal conditions. If any is missing, the relevant real-world intervention should stop. Description, candidate generation, evidence gathering, inaction, or proposals for reversible probes may continue; proposing an option does not itself authorize its implementation. These are necessary review items, not a guarantee that listing them automatically satisfies every domain's legal, professional, or safety requirements.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: definitional conventions, empirical assertions, mathematical consequences, and value commitments have different conditions for validity; a uniform label of ‘proven’ must not replace them.

  2. 2

    Decomposition: separate a compound statement into identifiable clauses and specify each clause's object and role; for H, also state whether it is empirical, operational, classificatory, or normative.

  3. 3

    Connection: definitions require semantic consistency; empirical claims require designs and materials; formal claims require premises and proofs; norms require values and reasons; action additionally requires permissions and stopping mechanisms. Satisfying one does not complete the rest.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: moving from ‘the explanation is credible’ to ‘action may be taken’ requires completing the action bridge; a missing component blocks only dispositions that depend on it, without automatically withdrawing independently established facts or proofs.

  5. 5

    Evidential responsibility: the framework's own D, C, or methodological descriptions must not serve as object facts; procedural compliance or normative justification must not be presented as proof of a causal mechanism.

Distinctions to keep clear

Semantic validity

An object fits a classification by definition.

≠

Empirical validity

The object and corresponding relations are supported by material, not generated by definition.

H domain marker

Indicates which kinds of additional contracts apply to human objects.

≠

Logical role

Further determine whether it is empirical, classificatory, procedural, or normative.

C outcome/mechanism contracts

Constrain how existing grounds may be used.

≠

Additional evidence

Requires independent materials and cannot increase merely through numbering.

Explanation/diagnosis

Describes what may happen and why.

≠

Authority to act

Qualification to take a specified action toward a target; it does not follow from depth of understanding.

Teaching construction: separating ‘accurate, therefore mandatory’Teaching scenario

AssumptionsThe tool, threshold e, and tests are hypothetical; they do not represent a real product or completed experiment.

Consider: ‘We define a tool with prediction error below e as accurate; tool A meets this criterion on a specified test set; therefore everyone should be compelled to use it, and its developers have the right to deploy it directly.’ The first sentence is a D-style semantic convention; the second is an empirical assertion whose test design and scope require checking; the ‘should be compelled’ in the third requires N-style value reasons, while deployment qualification requires authorization and O procedures. Neither follows from the error result. A proof of an algorithmic error bound would instead be an F-style conditional conclusion, and whether reality meets its assumptions would still need checking.

BoundaryUsed only to distinguish argumentative responsibilities; it does not establish any tool's reliability, justification, or permission for deployment.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: stipulating that ‘every operation called repair is beneficial’, then using an operation's registration as repair to prove that it is beneficial.

What it limitsThis inserts a normative conclusion into a definition and then supports it circularly; pre-specified goals, observed results, and value assessments should be separated.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: someone predicts a team's reactions most accurately and therefore claims permission to reassign its members.

What it limitsEpistemic advantage does not generate authorization; stop at explanation or a proposal rather than cross the permission boundary.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • A valid proof does not establish that a measurement mapping is true; passing a procedural check does not establish the existence of a substantive causal relation.
  • The action bridge is a minimal set of necessary conditions, not a complete administrative, medical, or legal permit; this lesson performs no real-world diagnosis or disposition.
  • Value premises may be criticized and revised, but renaming them ‘objective mechanisms’ must not exempt them from public justification.

Scope and open questions

This section provides argumentative roles and necessary bridging conditions; decomposing teaching statements directly demonstrates non-equivalence. Real-world cases cannot independently validate classificatory conventions, so historical facts are not forced into the lesson.

  1. 1

    ‘H6 is a normative boundary, so H1 also needs no empirical materials.’ Why does this inference fail?

  2. 2

    Does a formally supported instance define whether an effect is factually true or false?

  3. 3

    If stopping conditions are missing but an option is considered highly beneficial, does the bridge permit immediate implementation?

‘H6 is a normative boundary, so H1 also needs no empirical materials.’ Why does this inference fail?

H marks domain adaptation, not one uniform logical type. H1 is an empirical hypothesis requiring case-specific evidence; H6's normative status must not be transferred to it.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does a formally supported instance define whether an effect is factually true or false?

No. Instances and procedures govern how much support we may give; whether an effect exists in the world is the question they seek to answer, not something registration creates.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If stopping conditions are missing but an option is considered highly beneficial, does the bridge permit immediate implementation?

No. The relevant disposition should be suspended; options may be completed, a reversible probe proposed, or inaction retained. A judgment of benefit also requires its own evidence and normative reasons.

2.3Four Kinds of Dependency Must Be Kept Separate ​

In brief‘It is needed’ may mean that a conclusion cannot be inferred without it, cannot be published, applies only to a domain, or constrains action. Draw these four meanings separately, or procedures will be mistaken for causes and norms for evidence.

Relations between propositions use four different contracts. They must not be merged into an ambiguously defined “dependency.”

Kind of DependencyMeaningMay It Enter the Inferential Acyclic Graph?
inferential_requiresA hard inferential premise without which the conclusion cannot be obtainedYes
protocol_requiresMethod checks concerning evidence, causation, analogy, sources, or domain classificationNo
specializesRestricts a universal proposition to a particular domain, object, or subtypeNo
applies_toSpecifies which objects, propositions, or actions a norm or procedure applies toNo

Method checks determine whether a judgment may be released, but do not thereby become additional empirical causes. Domain specialization narrows the scope of application, but does not turn classification rules into factual evidence. Normative applicability constrains action, but does not in turn prove a description true. Only hard inferential premises enter the acyclic graph of roots and inferred conclusions.

2.3Note

Understanding this section

2.3 Four Types of Dependency Must Be Kept Separate

‘It is needed’ may mean that a conclusion cannot be inferred without it, cannot be published, applies only to a domain, or constrains action. Draw these four meanings separately, or procedures will be mistaken for causes and norms for evidence.

inferential_requires denotes a hard inferential premise: without it, the stated conclusion cannot be obtained in this disclosed argument. For example, inferring ‘all states with the same representation have the same target value, so a target-recovery function exists’ requires the premise that target values are constant across states sharing a representation. It may enter the directed acyclic root–conclusion graph, with direction consistently understood as running from a premise to the conclusion that depends on it.

protocol_requires denotes a method check: evidence, causal, analogy, source, or domain-classification contracts specify how this judgment must be recorded, examined, and published. A missing check removes the corresponding publication qualification, but the check is not an additional empirical cause in the world. Freezing beforehand provides a fixed basis for evaluation under the original question, while actual execution and deviations still need checking; a frozen document does not cause the physical effect.

specializes denotes specialization: restricting a general proposition to a domain, object, or subtype requires listing additional conditions and scope. It does not automatically establish the existence of the domain's object, nor turn classificatory clauses into supporting materials. applies_to records which subjects, actions, or propositions a norm or procedure constrains; a privacy rule applying to a record does not, in reverse, establish the truth of the facts claimed in that record.

The original table labels the four relations respectively ‘yes, no, no, no’ for entry into the inferential acyclic graph. This does not make the latter three unimportant; it requires separate graphs or layers to preserve their different meanings. A publication process may include cycles of review, return, and resubmission; this is procedural structure. Procedural cycles must not be misread as empirical-inference cycles merely to fit everything into a single DAG.

A case may involve multiple relations simultaneously, each of which should be recorded separately. A factual claim might inferentially use comparison data, face a freezing requirement for publication, be restricted to a subtype in scope, and be normatively constrained in action. It must not be represented by a single untyped ‘dependency’ edge. If a protocol check fails, first remove the corresponding publication or support qualification; if a hard premise fails, the inferred conclusion depending on it loses that basis. The two failures affect different things.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: different ‘dependencies’ pose different counterfactual questions: does removing it break the inference, disqualify publication, change scope, or make action impermissible?

  2. 2

    Classification: answer those questions for each edge and retain its relation type. A node may participate in several relation types, but sharing a name must not merge the meanings of its edges.

  3. 3

    Connection: hard inferential premises enter the root–conclusion DAG only where the validity of the conclusion is what is being explained. Methodological, specialization, and applicability relations are stored separately.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: layered graphs prevent inferring real mechanisms from publication requirements or real facts from normative applicability; they also identify which inferred conclusion should be suspended when a premise is compromised.

  5. 5

    Responsibility: registering a type is not itself proof; every hard premise still requires the corresponding derivation or materials, and method checks must be assessed against the actual contract.

Distinctions to keep clear

Inferentially necessary

Without this premise, this argument fails.

≠

Necessary for publication

If the procedure is unmet, the claim must not be published at that level; this does not directly change what is true or false in the world.

Domain specialization

Adds scope and conditions.

≠

Empirical support

Materials support specific relations in the specialized object; these two functions are not interchangeable.

Normative applicability

Specifies who or what must be constrained.

≠

Factual verification

Determines whether a particular description is supported; being protected does not mean the description is established.

Teaching construction: one conclusion about a recovery function and four relationsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDiscusses only a teaching setting involving sets, mappings, and a stipulated norm; it does not claim that any institution actually adopted the rule.

Proposition P: if π(x)=π(x′) always implies q(x)=q(x′), then g can be defined on the image of π such that q=g∘π. Set g(z) to the q value of any preimage; the constancy premise ensures that choosing a different preimage does not change the result, making it a hard inferential premise. Requiring disclosure of the state domain and checking records is a method check; restricting X to a finite set is a specialization; an institution's rule prohibiting use of g for unauthorized dispositions toward people is normative applicability. The latter three must not be treated as evidence establishing q's constancy.

BoundaryThe formal example supplies no real-world measurement sufficiency; publishing checking records also creates neither data nor authorization.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: ‘Publication requires ethical review, therefore ethical review is an empirical cause of the effect observed in the experiment.’

What it limitsThis misreads protocol_requires or applies_to as a causal mechanism. Procedures may constrain research behavior, but this permission relation does not itself establish the target physical or social effect.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: a procedural graph contains ‘failed review → revision → renewed review’, and this is used to declare the entire argument invalid through circularity.

What it limitsA procedural cycle is not an inferential cycle. Check the hard-premise DAG separately for cycles; the same judgment must not be applied indiscriminately across graph layers.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The acyclic-graph restriction concerns argumentative dependencies; it prohibits neither feedback in real systems nor review cycles in operational procedures.
  • A method check must not be deleted because it is absent from the inferential DAG: it still determines whether the corresponding conclusion may be published and used with a particular status.
  • If a condition initially treated as procedural is also written into a mathematical proposition's premises, separately register its formal role in that proposition and its role as a publication check; the two uses of the same wording must not silently collapse into one edge.

Scope and open questions

This section specifies dependency semantics; explicit mathematical examples and conditional counterexamples suffice to test the invalid inferences. Unrelated historical materials are not treated as empirical validation of graph types.

2.3.1Layered Responsibilities of the Common Method Kernel ​

In briefTwo theoretical texts may share requirements for careful recording and inference, but must not stamp one another as true. What is aligned is each layer's responsibilities and conditions, not names or numbers.

This framework and World Model may share methodological responsibilities, while each text retains its own objects, arguments, and mode of operation. Neither serves as an authoritative source or double empirical evidence for the other. Interoperation requires checking definitions, method constraints, formal propositions, empirical questions, outcome contracts, and governance requirements one by one. A shared name cannot substitute for a correspondence.

LayerQuestion AnsweredLimits of Its Force
DefinitionsWhat objects and terms refer toSpecify decidable semantics; do not establish that something holds in reality
Common method constraintsHow representations, the status of materials, and inference are governedConstrain recording and use; are not laws of the world
Conditional formal propositions FWhat necessarily follows under explicit mathematical premisesEstablished by proof; real-world mappings require separate verification
Empirical question families GWhether a specific empirical relation holdsInstances specify the object, comparison, mode of failure, and evidence
Outcome and mechanism contracts CWhat the existing basis permits to be registered and usedValid only within their dependencies, additional conditions, and applicable windows
Governance invariantsHow to release, evaluate, suspend, and actLimit power; do not serve as empirical causes

Identifiers such as D, G, and C provide stable references. The common kernel's Chinese identifiers serve only to align texts. They cannot replace the complete contracts in the body, nor can they obtain double support merely because another text uses the same name.

2.3.1Note

Understanding this section

2.3.1 Layered Responsibilities of the Common Method Kernel

Two theoretical texts may share requirements for careful recording and inference, but must not stamp one another as true. What is aligned is each layer's responsibilities and conditions, not names or numbers.

This section addresses the limits of interoperability between this framework and World Model: methodological responsibilities may be shared, while each text retains its own objects, arguments, and operational form. ‘May be shared’ does not mean correspondence has been verified across all versions. The current materials provide the current Xikari text, but not a full, identifiable version of World Model; this lesson therefore explains the declaration in this passage without claiming to have verified the other text.

The first layer in the original table, ‘definitions’, fixes assessable meanings for objects and terms; it can help the two texts establish what they are discussing, but does not prove that those objects exist in reality. The second layer, ‘common method constraints’, governs representations, the status of materials, and inference—for example, not treating simulations as observations or method checks as empirical causes. Shared adherence to these constraints creates no new natural or social law.

The third layer, F, answers what necessarily follows under mathematical premises. A proof's validity depends on its domain, mapping, target, operations, and assumptions; the same theorem name appearing in two texts does not eliminate the need to align premises and check proofs. The fourth layer, G, organizes specific empirical questions; actual support comes from instances with objects, comparisons, failure modes, and materials. Two texts retelling the same study do not constitute two independent observations.

The fifth layer, C, asks what existing grounds permit to be registered and used. It depends on relevant results, additional mechanistic conditions, and application windows; a rule's presence in the common kernel must not fill a missing mechanistic connection. The sixth layer, governance invariants, constrains publication, evaluation, suspension, and action; these limit the use of power and are not additional causes of changes in the research object.

D, G, and C numbers support stable references; the common kernel's Chinese numbering supports alignment across texts. Neither replaces a contract. Actual checking requires comparing complete meanings, premises, evidential statuses, targets, and failure rules side by side: record differences where the same name has different conditions, while differently named clauses with corresponding conditions may also admit a grounded mapping.

This section continues 2.2's argumentative roles and 2.3's dependency layers, preventing the circular move ‘I said it in another text too, so it has more support’. A common method may clarify interoperability; whether the framework is more useful for a class of real tasks remains a separate question requiring a comparison design and materials.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: the two texts each have their own object domains, operating forms, and arguments; repeated names do not imply identical premises and semantics.

  2. 2

    Connection one: comparing definitions, methods, F, G, C, and governance layer by layer distinguishes semantic compatibility, formal instances, empirical support, and limits on power.

  3. 3

    Connection two: reusing the same source adds no independent material, so agreement across texts cannot be totaled as double empirical support.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: shared methodological responsibilities can constitute interoperability requirements; whether particular texts satisfy the correspondence must be checked item by item after the correct versions are obtained.

  5. 5

    Responsibility and present limit: the current Xikari source supports this section’s description of its interface; it cannot by itself establish the actual content of World Model or that interoperability has operated successfully.

Distinctions to keep clear

Common method constraints

How both texts record and use grounds.

≠

Shared laws of the world

Empirical or formal claims about real-world regularities, requiring the corresponding proofs or materials.

Stable numbering

Makes contracts easier to locate.

≠

Complete contract

Meaning, premises, application window, evidence, and failure rules; numbering cannot replace them.

Agreement between two texts

May derive from shared definitions or the same materials.

≠

Two independent sources of empirical support

Require genuinely distinct materials or designs relevant to the claim; they must not be counted by document number.

A declaration of interoperability

Proposes checking responsibilities and possible ways of connecting.

≠

Verified interoperability

Actual versions, mappings, operations, and testing materials are all available for checking.

Teaching construction: identically named “closure” must be aligned condition by conditionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA and B are two texts constructed for teaching; they do not describe the actual content of World Model.

Suppose Text A’s “closure” requires only recovery of the current target q from representation π, while Text B’s “closure” additionally requires the representation to update on its own after every admissible action. The names match, but B adds dynamic and action conditions. Alignment should record “A requires static recovery; B has additional dynamic requirements,” rather than treating them interchangeably. Conversely, two different names may admit a formal mapping only when premises, domains, and conclusions are equivalent item by item.

BoundaryThe example illustrates an alignment method, not actual correspondence between books or any framework’s empirical effectiveness.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: two lectures cite the same study and then report “two independent studies support this.”

What it limitsRepeated retelling adds no original material; record the shared source and each interpretation without increasing the count of independent support.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Unresolved boundaryWithout obtaining the specified version of World Model, treating Xikari’s statement about shared methods as evidence of complete agreement between both texts.

What it limitsActual correspondence to the other text remains unchecked; Xikari’s own account can presently be explained, but the other text’s content cannot be supplied on its behalf.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • No identifiable version of the other text has been provided, so full terminological equivalence, full-text consistency, or an already shared operational kernel must not be claimed.
  • The six layers are not an evidential ladder that automatically upgrades from low to high. A definition does not become an empirical fact by passing through a methodological layer, and the governance layer is no better than empirical materials at establishing causation.
  • A failed correspondence between texts should restrict that particular connection; a mere difference in names should not invalidate all independently supported conclusions in the other text.

Scope and open questions

This section explains cross-text interfaces and argumentative responsibilities; unrelated historical facts are unsuitable validation. The specified version of the other text is currently absent, so a completed real cross-book case is not fabricated.

  • An actual interoperability comparison requires World Model’s author, complete version, date, and corresponding clauses; this guide only explains the requirements of the available Xikari source.
