2.4Causal Protocol[3] ​

In briefSeeing change after an action does not yet answer how much change the action caused. Conversely, a comparison answering the total-effect question may not identify every intermediate link.
Codes used in this section (2)
  • D3Scale Transformation
  • E5Testing Cross-Scale Transfer

A causal claim first registers the specific version of the treatment or cause, the outcome, the object and population, the time window, the scale, and the effect being asked about. It then explains why the comparison can identify that effect. Common inputs, selection, attrition, changes in measurement, reverse causation, and interference between units must all be addressed where relevant. A claim about a specified structural channel or a complete mediation mechanism must also provide the mechanism chain, temporal sequence, and discriminating evidence at that level: whether blocking, replacement, or natural variation meeting identification conditions changes outcomes as expected; whether alternative channels can explain the difference; whether cross-layer conclusions have a D3/E5 bridge; and what observations would make the mechanism claim fail.

Temporal sequence, correlation, and a coherent story cannot by themselves identify causation. A design may identify the total effect for a bounded population and window under explicit assumptions while still leaving the mediator undetermined. In that case, it should report “limited identification of the effect; the specific mechanism is unresolved.” Unsupported structural effects must not be filled in. Conversely, the separate existence of several local links does not automatically establish that the chain is connected as a whole in this case or that the net effect holds. Opposing paths may cancel one another out, and a total effect near zero does not establish that all mechanisms are absent. Causal strength, mechanism resolution, and the scope of extrapolation are evaluated separately.

2.4Note

Understanding this section

2.4 Causal Protocol

Seeing change after an action does not yet answer how much change the action caused. Conversely, a comparison answering the total-effect question may not identify every intermediate link.

A causal contract first specifies the treatment version and outcome. “Discontinuing a water source” differs from “issuing advice”; onset on a given day differs from death on that day; a local population differs from all city residents. Next fix the object, population, window, scale, and effect target. Without them, two studies calling something “effective” may answer entirely different questions.

Why the comparison identifies the target is central to a causal claim. A common input may affect treatment and outcome; self-selection makes recipients different at baseline; attrition changes the observed sample; measurement changes alter records; outcomes may influence treatment in reverse; one unit’s treatment may affect others. Address relevant issues individually rather than mechanically adding controls regardless of the task.

Identifying a total effect and identifying a specified structural channel carry different burdens. A claim that A affects Y through M needs the corresponding temporal order and mechanism chain, plus blocking, replacement, or natural variation meeting identification conditions that distinguish alternative explanations. Cross-level claims also check D3/E5 bridging. A design identifying only a total effect should not be forced to exhaust every microscopic process first; neither may the total effect fill in an untested mediator.

Evaluate causal strength, mechanism resolution, and extrapolation scope separately. A credible comparison within a bounded window does not establish a fine-grained account of every channel or transfer to every population. The reverse caution also matters: two mechanisms may offset, so a near-zero net total effect does not mean each mechanism is zero.

The next section, 2.4.1, distinguishes estimands such as “receiving an opportunity,” “accepting an intervention,” and “institutional expansion.” Section 2.4.2 uses an exact counterexample to show why accurate estimates of two average link effects still do not establish a composed whole-chain effect.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: causal questions include a counterfactual comparison of treatment and outcome; seeing only the realized path does not directly reveal the outcome on the path not taken.

  2. 2

    Connection: a credible design must explain why comparable groups, periods, or variation represent the target counterfactual and address confounding, selection, interference, and measurement issues relevant to that design.

  3. 3

    Conclusion: report a bounded total effect under the identification conditions; a specified mechanism also requires channel-discriminating evidence, and extrapolation requires additional bridging.

  4. 4

    Reverse check: a zero total effect may arise from offsetting paths; local paths may also exist without connecting in the same object and window.

  5. 5

    Evidential responsibility: historical documents support their actual observations and comparisons; narrative coherence does not automatically supply a net-effect estimate.

Distinctions to keep clear

Temporal order

A occurs before Y, satisfying one part of the required causal ordering.

≠

Causal identification

Can exclude or control the relevant competing explanations and support the specified counterfactual comparison.

Total effect

The combined change in the terminal outcome following a treatment change.

≠

Specified mechanism

Which channel produces change and under which common conditions.

Limited identification

Answers a question within a population, window, and set of assumptions.

≠

Broad extrapolation

Continued validity for new objects and scales requires additional grounds.

Mathematical teaching construction: two paths exactly offsetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth terms are additive components with the same units, object, and window, and the functions are fully given.

Let a∈{0,1}. One path adds a to the outcome and another subtracts a, giving terminal y(a)=a−a=0. Each constructed path varies with a, but y(1)−y(0)=0. This shows that the unconditional inference “zero net effect → no mechanisms exist” is invalid.

BoundaryOffsetting is stipulated, not estimated in a real system; changing units or adding interactions requires recalculation.

Broad Street: separate exposure evidence from the net effect of removing the handleDocumented case

Snow’s Table I for the 1854 Broad Street epidemic arranges fatal cases separately by onset date and death date: fatal-case onsets numbered 143 on September 1 and 28 on September 7; the pump handle was removed on September 8. The original also notes population departure and decline before discontinuation. This section adds the event-clock and counterfactual distinction: these records do not allow low values after removal to independently establish removal’s net effect.

SourceSnow, second edition, 1855, Table I and the author’s discussionPrinted page 49, Table I; post-table discussion on pages 50–52; page 40 records the September 7 meeting and handle removal the following dayReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe table includes cases with unknown onset dates and counts only eventually fatal cases. This guide estimates neither all infections nor a reconstructed control group and does not infer a zero effect of handle removal.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceSnow’s Table I records 143 fatal-case onsets on September 1 and 28 on September 7; the pump handle was removed only on September 8. The author also acknowledges a substantial decline before discontinuation.

What it limitsA decline already underway cannot all be attributed to later handle removal; neither does this establish that removal’s net effect must be zero.

John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera

What does not follow

  • Snow’s table contains separate columns for fatal cases arranged by onset date and counts by death date, not all infections or all cases of onset. Their denominators and event clocks must not be mixed.
  • Snow’s account of decline before discontinuation limits simple before-and-after attribution; it does not prove that removing the pump handle had no effect. Without a comparable counterfactual, a zero effect is not automatically identified either.
  • Retain the limited total-effect conclusion when a mechanism remains unidentified; when the total effect is not significant, retain independently grounded knowledge of local processes as well.

Scope and open questions

This historical case is used here only to identify temporal order, event definitions, and intervention-attribution boundaries, without repeating the preceding question about eligibility.

  • Estimating removal’s net effect would require a comparable counterfactual and materials on departure and changed water exposure; this guide does not turn a historical table into a randomized experiment.

2.4.1The Estimand and Mechanism Responsibilities ​

In briefAsk “what exactly changed?” before discussing effects. A lottery offering an opportunity, a person choosing uptake, and full institutional expansion involve different counterfactuals and cannot share one undifferentiated “treatment effect” label.

Offering someone an opportunity, that person actually receiving an intervention, and expansion of an entire institution are different treatments. A population average effect, the local average treatment effect for a particular kind of compliers, and each individual's outcome are also different estimands. When an identification assumption is impaired, downgrade only the conclusions that depend on it. For example, an interpretation based on a particular instrumental variable may no longer be reliable without automatically invalidating the effect of credible random assignment on “receiving an opportunity.”

More variables do not make observational control more reliable by default. Controlling for a mediator may change the total effect being asked about; controlling for a variable jointly determined by different causes may introduce bias. A larger sample cannot compensate for explanations that cannot be distinguished, either. When point identification is unavailable, supported bounds, sets of possible directions, exclusions based on necessary conditions, or specific process knowledge may be retained, with a clear statement of what these conclusions have not answered.

“Offering an opportunity” and “actually accepting, remaining, or exiting” are different treatments. The text of an agreement, verification, execution, and everyday use are also different outcomes. An announcement, public understanding, arrival, action at a border crossing, and full clearance must each be evidenced separately along the event chain. Neither a total effect nor the existence of an agreement can fill these gaps in mediation and distribution.

2.4.1Note

Understanding this section

2.4.1 Estimands and Mechanism Responsibilities

Ask “what exactly changed?” before discussing effects. A lottery offering an opportunity, a person choosing uptake, and full institutional expansion involve different counterfactuals and cannot share one undifferentiated “treatment effect” label.

Let Z denote receiving an opportunity, D actual uptake, and Y the outcome. Comparing randomized Z can identify the effect of offering the opportunity under the corresponding design conditions; directly comparing D=1 with D=0 may mix in self-selection. Even if Z changes D, additional conditions such as an exclusion restriction are needed to interpret the opportunity effect as a particular local effect of receiving treatment. When an additional assumption fails, withdraw the interpretation depending on it, without automatically withdrawing a still-credible randomized opportunity comparison.

The population average, the local average for a specified complier group, and each individual’s outcome answer different questions. A local effect may apply only to those whose uptake changes because the opportunity changes. It cannot directly generalize to never-takers, always-takers, all individuals, or full institutional expansion. Expansion may also change supply, congestion, interaction, and resource allocation, making the treatment version different.

More controls are not necessarily better. If the target is the total effect A→M→Y, holding M fixed changes the question. Controlling a variable jointly affected by A and other causes can also open an association that was previously absent. First specify variables’ positions in the generating process rather than adding every correlated variable to a regression. Even a larger sample does not remove indistinguishability produced by the design.

Failure of point identification does not require pretending to know everything or nothing. Retain bounds, sets of possible directions, exclusions by necessary conditions, or specific process knowledge supported by assumptions and material, and list the unanswered targets. Partial identification must actually follow from the corresponding constraints; assigning an arbitrary interval does not make it rigorous.

The source closes with common event substitutions: agreement text, verification, execution, and everyday use are not the same thing. An announcement, public understanding, arrival, border handling, and full clearance likewise cannot have one node stand for the entire chain. Each changed treatment or outcome definition requires rechecking its event, time, object, and dependency route.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Target definition: let ITT_Y=E[Y|Z=1]−E[Y|Z=0], the mean difference grouped by opportunity Z; the design must explain randomization, outcome comparability, attrition, and related conditions.

  2. 2

    Additional conditions: if Z is randomized, actually changes D, affects Y only through D, has no defiers, and satisfies consistency and the corresponding no-interference conditions, then in the binary case ITT_Y／(E[D|Z=1]−E[D|Z=0]) can be interpreted as the local average effect for compliers.

  3. 3

    Limitation: failure of conditions such as the exclusion restriction or monotonicity undermines this interpretation as a local effect of receipt. It does not automatically establish that the effect of the opportunity assigned by randomized Z is also absent.

  4. 4

    Change of use: moving from a local effect of receipt to population-wide expansion, manipulation of a particular mediator, or individual prediction requires the corresponding additional assumptions and material; changing the title is insufficient.

  5. 5

    Evidential responsibility: in this lesson the historical Oregon example supports only the design distinction that “randomly offering an opportunity to apply does not randomly guarantee enrollment.” The formula is a teaching explanation under explicit assumptions, not a substitute for all identification checks in the paper.

Distinctions to keep clear

Receiving an opportunity Z

Can be compared through random assignment.

≠

Actual uptake D

Affected by eligibility, choice, and execution; not necessarily random.

Local average effect

Average change for a specified group of compliers.

≠

Population or individual effect

Needs a different target and identification basis; it cannot be read directly from a local average.

Failure of point identification

The target quantity cannot be uniquely determined.

≠

No information at all

A stronger claim; bounds, directions, or process constraints may remain.

Mathematical teaching construction: one ratio, two layers of assumptionsTeaching scenario

Assumptions2 and 0.25 are purely teaching assumptions, not observed values from the Oregon paper. Units and the time window are fixed.

Suppose a randomly assigned opportunity increases the average outcome by 2 units and increases the receipt rate by 0.25, and additionally suppose the binary IV conditions above hold. The local average effect for compliers is then 2÷0.25=8 units. If the opportunity also directly affects Y, the numerator includes a path that does not run through D, so 8 loses that interpretation. If random assignment of the opportunity, measurement, and other relevant conditions still hold, 2 can still represent the opportunity effect.

BoundaryThis calculation cannot establish the exclusion restriction or monotonicity in reality, nor assign 8 to every individual.

Mathematical teaching construction: controlling a common outcome can create an associationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsIndependent, equally probable binary variables and deterministic functions are explicitly constructed assumptions.

Let A and U be independent binary variables taking 0 and 1, and define S=A+U and Y=U. A does not affect Y in the population. Restricting the sample to S=1 leaves only (A,U)=(1,0) and (0,1), so those with A=1 have Y=0 and those with A=0 have Y=1: a negative association appears. Controlling the common outcome S changes the sample structure.

BoundaryThis counterexample rejects only “more controls necessarily mean greater reliability.” It does not imply that all controls are bad and is not an empirical estimate.

Oregon’s 2008 lottery: selection offered an opportunity to applyDocumented case

The official abstract of the 2011 NBER working paper states that in 2008 a group of uninsured low-income Oregon adults obtained the opportunity to apply for Medicaid through a lottery. The design itself distinguishes winning an opportunity from actually becoming insured; the former cannot be renamed universal receipt of an identical intervention.

What does not follow

  • Controlling another variable may change the target or introduce bias; more observations improve some estimation precision but do not automatically repair identification.

Scope and open questions

An actual lottery study directly illustrates the distinction between opportunity and receipt. Only design facts from the official abstract obtained are used here; formal derivation is separately labeled as teaching material.

2.4.2Local Effects, Joint Responses, and the Chain as a Whole ​

In briefTwo average effects can both be real and still produce no effect when connected: people changed by the first stage may be precisely those who do not respond to the second. Joint responses in the same objects are crucial.

When local channels are combined, the correspondence between an earlier output and a later input, the identity of the same case and its temporal sequence, the common scope of support, joint responses, and terminal outcomes should be retained. Even when two studies concern the same population, their two average effects generally cannot be multiplied directly: the people whose mediator changes may be precisely those whose outcome would not respond to that mediator. Accurate averages on both sides do not guarantee that the common conditions needed for the sequence have been retained.

A finite counterexample is a population composed of two equally weighted types, with type denoted by s∈{0,1}, binary treatment by a, and mediator by m. Let m(a)=a(1−s), with outcome y(a,m)=sm. The average effect of treatment on the mediator and the average effect of directly setting the mediator on the outcome are both 1/2. Yet in each type, the effect of treatment on the final outcome is 0, and the effect of the chain as a whole is 0. Multiplying the two averages gives 1/4, which is not the effect of the chain as a whole. This is a counterexample under given functions. It neither estimates a real-world effect nor denies a total effect independently identified by a qualified design.

“Complete” in a claim about the chain as a whole is relative only to the declared outcome, window, and dependency route. If the purpose is to identify a particular total effect with a specified scope, there is no requirement to exhaust all microscopic processes first. If the purpose changes to manipulating a mediator, transferring across domains, or allocating responsibility, supply the connections on which that purpose actually depends. Shared resources, offsetting paths, and feedback can change the result of the connection. Separate evidence for each node cannot substitute for a joint test in the same case.

2.4.2Note

Understanding this section

2.4.2 Local effects, joint responses, and the whole chain

Two average effects can both be real and still produce no effect when connected: people changed by the first stage may be precisely those who do not respond to the second. Joint responses in the same objects are crucial.

Serial composition must preserve more than two averages. Does the first stage's output match the actual version of the second stage's input? Can the same objects and sequence be matched? Do the stages share a support range? Who responds to both? What is the terminal outcome? These joint conditions determine whether the chain connects. Different studies may indeed be incompatible, but even within the same population, losing the joint structure can still produce error.

The original gives a complete finite counterexample. s=0 and s=1 each have weight one half; treatment a and mediator m are binary; m(a)=a(1−s), y(a,m)=sm. Treatment changes the mediator for those with s=0, but they do not respond to the mediator. Those with s=1 respond to the mediator, but treatment does not change their mediator. The two stages' effects occur in different people.

The local average A→M is therefore 1/2, and the average M→Y under external assignment of M is also 1/2. Under the actual composition m(a), each type's terminal outcome is always 0, making the whole-chain effect 0. The product of averages, 1/4, differs from the average product of individual responses, 0. The given functions refute unconditional multiplication; they do not estimate the effect of any actual mechanism.

“Complete” is relative to a target, window, and dependency route. Identifying a bounded total effect need not require knowledge of every microscopic link. Manipulating a mediator, transferring across domains, or allocating responsibility requires the connections on which that use depends. Shared resources, counteracting paths, and feedback can change the composite outcome. Evidence for each node separately cannot be recast as an established whole chain within the same case.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: P(s=0)=P(s=1)=1/2; m(a)=a(1−s), y(a,m)=sm; change a from 0 to 1.

  2. 2

    First stage: Δm=m(1)−m(0)=1−s, equal to 1 when s=0 and 0 when s=1, so E[Δm]=1/2.

  3. 3

    Second stage: hold a fixed and externally set m from 0 to 1. Then Δ_my=y(a,1)−y(a,0)=s, with mean E[Δ_my]=1/2.

  4. 4

    Whole chain: y(a,m(a))=s·a(1−s)=0 because binary s satisfies s(1−s)=0. Hence y(1,m(1))−y(0,m(0)) is 0 for both types, and its mean remains 0.

  5. 5

    Incorrect multiplication: E[1−s]E[s]=1/4, whereas E[(1−s)s]=0. Discarding the correspondence between the two stage responses changes the quantity being calculated.

  6. 6

    Conclusion and responsibility: this counterexample suffices to refute the universal claim that “two average effects can always be multiplied.” Multiplication in another model requires separate proof of structure, homogeneity, or appropriate joint conditions. The example cannot negate a total effect identified by an independent qualified design.

Distinctions to keep clear

Average edge effect

The effect of each stage averaged separately across the population.

≠

Whole-chain effect

The terminal difference arising from actual sequential connection within the same object.

Evidence for individual nodes

Each local fact has corresponding grounds.

≠

Evidence for joint connections

Versions, identities, timing, and joint responses are compatible in this case.

A complete bounded chain

Covers the connections on which the current use actually depends.

≠

Exhausting every mechanism

This is not required to identify every bounded total effect.

Mathematical construction from the original: two nonoverlapping response typesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn exact binary domain, two equally weighted types, and deterministic functions specified in the original, without random error or sampling.

Complete two-type table: when s=0, m(0)=0, m(1)=1, and y(a,0)=y(a,1)=0; when s=1, m(0)=m(1)=0, y(a,0)=0, and y(a,1)=1. Each type has terminal outcome 0 under the corresponding composition. With equal weights, both edge averages are 0.5, while the actual whole-chain average is 0.

BoundaryThis expands the original formal counterexample; it is not an observational study and supplies no proportions or effects for an actual population.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleIn the original counterexample, one group responds only at the first stage and the other only at the second. Both edge averages are 1/2; the whole chain is 0.

What it limitsLimits unconditional “multiplication of average edges”: joint responses must be retained. It does not affect a separately identified total effect.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • This counterexample is calculated exactly from the original text's specified functions. It cannot establish that all real mediation analyses are invalid, nor negate a total effect identified through another qualified design.
  • Multiplication may hold if both stage responses are constant across people, or if sufficient structural conditions make the desired whole-chain quantity exactly equal the product of means. These are additional conditions, not consequences of the two means themselves.
  • Changing the treatment version, permitted mediator manipulation, or terminal target requires rewriting the calculation. Equal numerical values do not mean equal contracts.

Scope and open questions

This section uses a complete finite counterexample to refute a universal inference; the mathematical construction directly completes that task. No forced real-world example is added to simulate empirical confirmation.

  1. 1

Why does “the same population” still not guarantee that the two stage averages can be multiplied?

Responses may be heterogeneous even within the same population. One must know whether first- and second-stage responses overlap in the same objects.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Is the second stage's 1/2 in this example an average outcome observed under actual m(a)?

No. It is the average response to externally setting m from 0 to 1. Under actual composition, a does not change m for those with s=1.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Must finding this kind of composition problem revoke a bounded total effect from an independent randomized trial?

No. Failure of a compositional inference and the total effect from another qualified design have different grounds. Retain or downgrade each according to its own dependencies.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

2.4.3Constitutive Relations and Causal Relations ​

In briefWhether a right or eligibility is established and whether it is realized are two questions requiring separate answers.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • G2Specified-Channel Effects and Per-Dimension Boundedness

Some relations specify what a thing counts as under a given set of rules: whether an expression becomes a commitment, whether a document becomes a valid authorization, whether a person holds membership or eligibility to apply. Constitutive relations of this kind answer whether a standing holds. Their grounds are the source of the rule, the party entitled to perform the act, the required form, and the argument that the rule applies to the present case; they are not established by estimating effects. Causal questions ask what actually happened after the standing came to hold: whether rights were honored, whether commitments were fulfilled, whether eligibility changed opportunities and behavior.

The two kinds of question are evidenced separately, and neither can pay in place of the other. A causal role that has not yet been identified does not cancel a standing that has already come to hold under the rules; nor does the holding of a standing prove that the corresponding effects have occurred. When analyzing the same arrangement, keep at least four items separate: whether the constitutive conditions are met, whether the parties understand it this way, whether it is executed and honored in practice, and whether it is normatively justified. A right may already be valid and not yet be honored; understanding a request is not the same as acknowledging that it has the standing to enter the decision.

A constitutive standing holds under the rules of the object's own domain and is supported by sources of law, documents, and records of acts by those entitled to perform them; the status of these materials is handled under §2.1.1. It is different from this framework's definition D, nor does it belong to the question of channel effects under G2. Pointing out that a standing is constituted by rules does not mean that all objects arise from convention, nor that the rules making the classification are thereby neutral or justified. Section 5.5.5 separates the de facto existence of an institution from its legal validity; the latter belongs to the constitutive question here. For the corresponding distinctions concerning forms of meaning and authorization, see §7.3.3 and §14.6.

2.4.3Note

Understanding this section

2.4.3 Constitutive and Causal Relations

Whether a right or eligibility is established and whether it is realized are two questions requiring separate answers.

A constitutive relation asks whether, under applicable rules and valid conditions, this act constitutes appointment, commitment, a right, or a decision. First check the rule's source, the authorized subject, required form, and specific applicability. Recognition of status need not first identify a causal effect changing behavior.

A causal relation then asks whether established status changes actions, resources, or outcomes through a channel. Constitutive evidence can help establish who has which status, but cannot prove actual fulfillment. Effects that have occurred cannot retroactively repair an invalid procedure either.

Keep four columns separate when reading: constitutive conditions, participants' understandings, actual implementation or realization, and normative justification. They can yield different answers. A right may be validly established but not yet realized; an actual arrangement may be effective while lacking legal status or justification.

This is not an ontological claim that all objects arise from convention. It explains the division of evidential responsibilities and should be read alongside §5.5.5: the connection here concerns legal validity, which cannot be absorbed into the question of an institution's factual existence.

Terms used here

Constitutive relation
Explains how a status is established under applicable rules.
Causal relation
Explains how a change affects subsequent outcomes through a channel.

From the source

The two kinds of question are evidenced separately, and neither can pay in place of the other.

2.5Evidence Protocol ​

In brief“Having a source” answers only where material comes from, not what it establishes. Evidence is a support relation directed at a specific claim, requiring an account of why every step connects.

The evidence chain distinguishes sources, materials, observation records, evidence, counterexamples, judgments, and authorization to act. Each layer needs its own justification for conversion. Register the object, data-generation process, research design, measurement and selection, uncertainty, competing explanations, and limits of extrapolation according to the specific task. Formal root instances and foresight[4] must also register null models, thresholds, and evaluation under their own contracts. A material's having a source does not permit omitting the support relation between that material and the current claim.

Absence and silence are not negative evidence by default; inability to observe is not the same as nonexistence. Justified opacity must state its reason, minimum scope, duration, and trusted reviewer, with the strength of public conclusions reduced accordingly. If counterexamples or residuals are found after evidence has been frozen, the failure record should be retained, and the claim downgraded, suspended, or withdrawn under the contract. The object, subtype, threshold, or success criterion must not be rewritten after results appear.

2.5Note

Understanding this section

2.5 Evidence protocol

“Having a source” answers only where material comes from, not what it establishes. Evidence is a support relation directed at a specific claim, requiring an account of why every step connects.

A source is a person, archive, instrument, or study; material is the text, signal, or data left behind; an observation record is a result organized by rules; evidence is those records' support for a claim. A counterexample challenges a particular claim; judgment combines grounds and uncertainty; authorization for action separately determines what may be done on that basis. One cannot leap from “a reliable institution exists” at the beginning to “I have authority to intervene” at the end.

Record, as appropriate to the task, the object, material-generation process, research design, measurement and selection, uncertainty, competing explanations, and extrapolation boundaries. A material's use may change its support relation: a notice can directly establish what its text says, but cannot alone show that the public understood, personnel implemented it, or outcomes improved. Formal root instances and foresight must also register N0, thresholds, and evaluation under their respective contracts. Do not fabricate a G contract for an ordinary historical text merely to make the form look complete.

Absence and silence have no default direction. An event's absence from a log may mean it did not occur, was not recorded, its record was lost, the record is inaccessible, or disclosure is prohibited. Corresponding negative information arises only when the event should demonstrably have left a detectable record. Evidential force against occurrence varies with recording and retrieval capability; the words “not found” do not automatically make it strong.

Protective nondisclosure is not an unconditional exemption from review. State the protective grounds, minimum scope, duration, and credible reviewer, and reduce the strength of conclusions that cannot be publicly supported. If no credible review is possible at all, privacy cannot become a pass for strong factual claims. Nor should unnecessary sensitive disclosure be compelled merely to complete a field.

When counterexamples and residuals appear after freezing, preserve the original record and downgrade, suspend, or withdraw according to the contract. Objects, subtypes, thresholds, and success criteria cannot be rewritten afterward as “we really intended a different question.” A new question may receive a separate version; the old failure remains under its original contract.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: material generation and visibility determine which possible situations it can distinguish. Authentic provenance does not ensure that measurement fits the target.

  2. 2

    Connection: material becomes bounded evidence only by stating, item by item, “why this record supports this claim, and which alternative explanations it remains compatible with.”

  3. 3

    Reverse check: if the same absence could result either from nonoccurrence or from nonrecording, absence cannot uniquely support nonoccurrence.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: register evidence strength, competing explanations, and failures by claim. Opacity and missingness limit the corresponding conclusions rather than automatically eliminating all existing material.

  5. 5

    Authorization responsibility: moving from judgment to action still requires norms, lawful authorization, an action ceiling, and stopping conditions. A chain of sources does not itself create authority.

Distinctions to keep clear

Locatable provenance

The material and version can be found.

≠

Explicit support relation

One can explain how the material supports the specific claim and what it still cannot exclude.

No record

Nothing was found within the specified material and search scope.

≠

Records establish absence

Requires a sufficiently reliable mechanism by which traces should be left and detected.

Protective nondisclosure

Has explicit protective grounds, narrow scope, duration, and credible review.

≠

A claim exempt from review

No such exemption exists; inability to review requires downgrading.

Teaching construction: what does a blank log actually exclude?Teaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth logging systems are teaching assumptions; no claim is made that actual logs are 100% reliable.

Suppose an event always causes the system to generate and retain a retrievable record, and the query scope is complete. Under these conditions, “no record” can count against occurrence. Now suppose the recorder operates only when connected, and the target period may include a network outage. The same blank cannot distinguish nonoccurrence from occurrence unrecorded during an outage. What changed is the material-generation condition, not the researcher's preferred answer.

BoundaryActual evidential force against occurrence requires material on recording rates, retention policies, permissions, and search coverage. It cannot inherit certainty from this construction.

2.5.1Measurement Objects and Data Generation ​

In briefA score can be calculated very accurately without measuring what you actually care about. Measurement asks first about the target and data generation, then about error magnitude and comparability.

Directly recorded quantities, composite indicators defined by construction, measurement of latent attributes, formative conditions, and predictive proxies carry different explanatory responsibilities. A test score can accurately reflect performance within the current set of questions while not yet representing long-term capability. Usage can fall while the required services are still insufficient. More diagnoses may also reflect easier access to testing. First state what is to be measured and how the materials are generated, then decide which errors and counterexamples are relevant to the current use.

Comparisons across groups or periods require comparability proportionate to the task. Estimating latent means generally requires explaining the unit and origin of the measurement scale. Person-specific threshold decisions must also address individual error and consequences. An identical scoring mapping does not establish identical psychological strategies. If the common anchors themselves drift, more samples may not distinguish genuine change from changes in the measurement scale. External anchoring should be sought, or sensitivity reported.

Changes in an indicator can result from genuine improvement, genuine adaptation to a narrow target, changes in the sample that enters or is reported, or falsification of records. These mechanisms can coexist and require separate investigation. Nor does the fact that two legitimate indicators answer different questions and point in opposite directions mean that one must be wrong, much less justify directly concluding that there has been manipulation.

2.5.1Note

Understanding this section

2.5.1 Measurement Objects and Data Generation

A score can be calculated very accurately without measuring what you actually care about. Measurement asks first about the target and data generation, then about error magnitude and comparability.

The source distinguishes five kinds of object. Directly recorded quantities, such as counts under an established protocol, still entail responsibility for missed records and event definitions. Definitional composite indicators combine components by rule; correct calculation does not establish a latent attribute that the indicator reflects. Latent-attribute measurement must explain the model relating observable indicators to an attribute not directly visible, alternatives and validation. Formative conditions concern conditions that jointly constitute or affect the target; they need not rise and fall together as reflective indicators of one attribute would. A predictive proxy only needs predictive capability for a future target; it does not thereby become a direct measure of another target.

Thus a test score can reliably record performance in the current item domain without fully representing long-term capability. Declining service use may indicate unmet needs, and increasing diagnoses may result from easier detection rather than more disease. These are different data-generation paths; observing one direction must not automatically select the most appealing story.

Comparisons across groups or periods must fit the purpose. Estimating latent means requires interpretable correspondence in scale units and origins; making person-level threshold decisions also requires analysis of individual error and consequences. Using the same scoring formula in two groups does not establish identical item meanings, response strategies or measurement relations. If shared anchors drift, larger samples may only estimate the same unidentified problem more precisely; seek external anchors or perform sensitivity analysis.

Improvement in an indicator may have at least four causes: genuine improvement in the target; behavior that adapts to a narrow metric without improving the broader target; changes in sample or reporting composition; or fabricated records. These mechanisms can coexist, but indicator change alone must not trigger accusations of fabrication. Two valid indicators can also move in opposite directions while both being correct if one measures a total and the other a subgroup.

The actual algorithm case illustrates proxy mismatch: costs were the predicted label, and the study compared costs and health burdens across groups at the same risk score. Similar cross-group cost calibration does not mean small individual prediction errors or good aggregate prediction accuracy. When identifying care needs, the relationship between cost and need must also be validated as comparable in the target groups. Reconsidering the label does not declare all proxies invalid; it requires evidence of fit for the current purpose.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: observed scores are jointly generated by the target attribute, measurement rules, opportunities for contact, selection and recording processes; different generation processes can produce the same score.

  2. 2

    Classification: first register whether the measurement concerns a direct quantity, definitional composite, latent attribute, formative condition or predictive proxy, and identify which errors affect its current use.

  3. 3

    Connection: accurate prediction of a label directly supports only that label's task; using it to judge need, capability or value requires separate evidence connecting measurement and purpose.

  4. 4

    Comparison conditions: when groups or times change, check units, origins, anchors, individual errors and sample composition; an identical formula does not imply identical psychological processes.

  5. 5

    Conclusion: when reporting indicator changes, retain competing generation mechanisms and propose discriminating checks; without sufficient materials, do not promote one explanation into fact.

Distinctions to keep clear

Predicting a label accurately

The model predicts the explicitly specified target well.

≠

Measuring the attribute actually of concern

The label's relationship to the target attribute and intended use has been checked.

Definitional composite indicator

The components and weights define the score's composition.

≠

Latent-attribute measurement

Requires an argument for how observed indicators reflect the latent attribute and for their comparability.

Formative conditions

The conditions may move in different directions while jointly affecting or constituting the target.

≠

Reflective indicators

Represent manifestations of a latent attribute within the model and require a different testing logic.

Indicators move in opposite directions

This may result from different objects, denominators, weights or tasks.

≠

The data must be fabricated

Requires independent evidence; different directions do not directly imply fabrication.

Mathematical teaching construction: a changing mean or a drifting scale originTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn additive measurement model, common units and no other error; used only to illustrate identifiability.

Assume an observed score S=θ+b, where θ is the attribute to be measured and b the scale origin. An observed mean rising from 4 to 6 over two periods could reflect θ increasing by 2 with b unchanged, or unchanged θ with b increasing by 2. Observing S alone cannot distinguish them. Even infinitely large samples and error-free observed means in each period still require external anchoring or testable constraints to interpret the change.

BoundaryNot measured facts about any scale or population; a particular measurement relation may be nonlinear and require a different model.

Teaching construction: two correct indicators can move in opposite directionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCase counts are stipulated for teaching, and event definitions and windows are comparable; there is no sampling or underreporting.

A service handles 10 cases in the first period, of which 2 are overdue, then 30 in the second, of which 3 are overdue. The total overdue count rises from 2 to 3, while the rate falls from 20% to 10%. Both calculations are correct: one answers total burden, the other the proportion of cases. Opposite directions alone cannot establish fabrication by either side.

BoundaryThis does not establish improvement in a real service; case difficulty, demand and people not served in the second period may still affect evaluation.

The 2019 study of a cost-prediction algorithm: proxy and need are different targetsDocumented case

Obermeyer et al. analyzed data from a large academic hospital during 2013–2015. The audited algorithm predicted healthcare costs. At the same risk score, the study found similar costs in the following year for the two groups but a heavier health burden among Black patients. This indicates more consistent cross-group cost calibration, not necessarily high aggregate or individual prediction accuracy; calibration also cannot replace a test of fitness for care needs.

Scope and limitsInterpret the paper within its specific sample, indicators and purpose. This guide has not recalculated individual data, makes no individual medical judgment and does not claim that changing the label has improved actual long-term outcomes.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceThe study shows similar next-year costs in the two groups at the same risk score, indicating relatively consistent cross-group cost calibration, while Black patients have a heavier health burden.

What it limitsThis limits the inference that “consistent cross-group cost calibration fairly identifies health needs”; it does not establish high individual cost-prediction accuracy or invalidate the cost-prediction task itself.

Obermeyer et al., Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations

Teaching counterexampleIn the teaching construction, scale-origin drift and genuine attribute change produce the same observed change in means.

What it limitsMore observations of the same kind cannot alone identify the two mechanisms; add anchoring or make sensitivity explicit.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The Obermeyer study evaluates an algorithm in a particular hospital and a 2013–2015 sample; it must not be used to judge unexamined individuals or all current models.
  • Observed differences in group calibration do not mean every social mechanism has been disentangled; changing a label also does not automatically guarantee long-term health benefits or fulfillment of all fairness norms.
  • High internal consistency, an identical formula or a larger sample cannot alone guarantee a latent-attribute measure's construct validity and cross-group fit.

Scope and open questions

The primary paper directly examines mismatch between prediction labels and health needs, fitting this section's distinction between measurement objects and proxy uses.

  • Transferring this conclusion to another institution or current algorithm requires that version's labels, data-generation process, group comparability and actual outcome materials.

No. Stability is one property; construct content, generalization beyond the item domain, measurement relations and fitness for use still require argument.

2.6Analogy Protocol ​

In briefThe most useful role of “this resembles something else” is to suggest what to investigate next; it cannot directly import that other thing's causes, evaluations and solutions.

Analogy is only a tool for generating questions. Every use must be explicitly marked as an analogy and specify the source domain, target domain, shared structure, key differences, nontransferable conditions, variable mapping, and discriminating tests. Similar words, similar diagrams, compelling narratives, or similar outcomes do not constitute evidence for a bridge across domains.

Analogy can help ask “which channel, boundary, or competing explanation should also be checked.” It cannot replace a G-instance, nor can it transfer causal relations, normative evaluations, or action plans directly from the source domain to the target domain. If contrary conditions have not been specified, the conclusion from the analogy remains a heuristic candidate.

2.6Note

Understanding this section

2.6 Analogy Protocol

The most useful role of “this resembles something else” is to suggest what to investigate next; it cannot directly import that other thing's causes, evaluations and solutions.

An adequate analogy lists at least the source domain, target domain, shared structure, key differences, nontransferable conditions, variable mapping and discriminating tests, and explicitly calls itself an analogy in the main text. Comparing a queue to stored water, for example, may share an “inflow, stock, outflow” structure. But people can leave, change choices or respond strategically, and water volume and numbers of people must not be combined without specifying units and processes.

A variable mapping turns “similarity” from rhetoric into a checkable proposal: which source-domain quantity corresponds to which target-domain quantity, under which operations the relationship persists, and when it fails. Similar diagrams, identical words, appealing stories and similar outcomes do not complete this mapping. Treating “organizational immunity” or “social temperature” as measured mechanisms exemplifies the overreach to avoid.

An analogy can generate a checklist: which source-domain channels, boundaries or competing explanations merit investigation in the target domain? But empirical causal relations in the source do not automatically become target-domain facts. Corresponding operations, measurements and alternative explanations still need testing in the target, and analogy cannot replace formal G-instance requirements.

Contrary conditions must actually constrain the claim. If researchers say “it still looks similar” regardless of what they observe, the analogy cannot eliminate mistaken candidates. A reasonable formulation states that particular target-domain behavior, object identities or resource constraints invalidate the mapping; if discriminating tests are incomplete, retain only a heuristic candidate. Normative evaluations and action plans particularly must not transfer directly on resemblance alone.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: known relations in the source domain depend on its particular objects, variables and operating conditions; similarity covers only some of these.

  2. 2

    Connection: writing down mappings and differences first permits judgment of which source-domain questions can be target-domain candidates and which observations would invalidate the mapping.

  3. 3

    Conclusion: analogy permits asking questions and generating relations for testing, not directly declaring that target-domain mechanisms, value judgments or actions are established.

  4. 4

    Evidential responsibility: target-domain support must come from its own materials and bridges; even reliable source-domain research cannot fill in unobserved conditions in the target.

  5. 5

    Responsibility for failure: retain dissimilarities and counterevidence; mapping failures must not be explained away as target-domain “anomalies” while the analogy is never revised.

Distinctions to keep clear

Structural similarity

Some relations or indicators can correspond.

≠

Identical mechanism

Identical causal processes and operating conditions require new discriminating evidence.

Generating questions

Deciding what to investigate first.

≠

Confirming answers

Which relations the materials can already support has a different evidential force.

Evaluation within an analogy

A judgment reached under the source domain's value criteria.

≠

Justification in the target domain

Targets, rights, risks and authorization must be made explicit anew.

Teaching analogy: when a queue stops resembling stored waterTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThis is an explicitly labeled teaching analogy; no real queue has been observed. The target domain must declare its own units and event rules.

The source domain is a water tank and the target a service queue. Mapping inflow to new arrivals, water level to queue length and outflow to completed service can generate the question to investigate: “Does the stock accumulate when arrivals exceed processing capacity?” But if people can leave midway, obtain duplicate queue numbers or decide not to arrive after seeing a long queue, additional channels are needed. Record arrivals, completions, exits and duplicate counts to test which conservation equation applies, rather than directly substituting tank parameters for a population.

BoundaryThe analogy does not establish service effectiveness, still less that people should be controlled like water; empirical and normative conditions in the target domain require separate checks.

A 2022 ancient-DNA study's explicit limits on resemblance to great apesDocumented case

Skov et al. compared patterns of genetic diversity when studying Neanderthal communities, but explicitly warned in “Inferring social organization” that similar ratios of Y-chromosome to mitochondrial coalescence times do not necessarily imply the same social organization; multiple scenarios can produce similar statistics.

SourceSkov et al., Genetic insights into the social organization of NeanderthalsNature 610 (2022), 519–525; PMC main text, Inferring social organization, the cautionary paragraph following the comparison of 47 human populations and 10 great-ape subspecies (this guide does not use its specific comparative values)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the authors' limitation on analogy is used; ancient DNA is not used to evaluate modern groups, and their demographic-history model is not recalculated.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceSkov et al.'s 2022 study explicitly warns that similar Y-chromosome/mitochondrial coalescence-time ratios in Neanderthals and great apes do not necessarily imply identical social organization; multiple scenarios can produce similar ratios.

What it limitsA real study itself distinguishes statistical resemblance from social explanation; similar indicators must not be used to bypass generation mechanisms.

Skov et al., Genetic insights into the social organization of Neanderthals

What does not follow

  • In actual research, similar statistics can result from different formation processes; two similar numbers cannot establish identical social institutions.
  • An analogy need not match in every respect to be useful, but the part claimed to transfer must be explicit; stop using it or narrow it when differences affect key premises.
  • This guide does not use biological analogies to assign standing, personality or governance arrangements to actual individuals or groups.

Scope and open questions

The primary study explicitly states that similar indicators cannot replace evidence of social mechanisms, directly illustrating the ceiling on analogy's applicability.

No. Similar-looking diagrams do not reveal the meaning of edges, actual flows, permissions, or alternative channels. Materials from the target domain must be checked.

If an analogy faces counterevidence but can still inspire a question, must it be discarded entirely?

Not necessarily. Restrict or remove the failed part while retaining insights that clearly remain applicable. The original strong mechanism conclusion must not be retained.

2.6.1Analogy, Formal Instances, and Tested Comparisons ​

In briefResembling something, belonging to the same class within a model, and being supported in the target world are three different statuses. Keeping them separate neither devalues analogy nor lends it evidential force it has not acquired.

A heuristic analogy, a formal instance satisfying explicit mathematical premises, and a target-domain relation tested against independent materials are three different states. For the first, state similarities and differences; for a formal instance, check variables and assumptions; for empirical transfer, test operations, formation processes, and alternative explanations in the target domain. A comparison supported by independent evidence can contribute to a specific argument. Its support comes from those materials and bridges, not from the word “like.”

Historical and archaeological comparisons must also distinguish the physical formation of traces, the functions of activities, and social relations. Similar tool marks do not automatically imply the same institutions of power; kinship does not automatically imply relations of rule; and accurate dates do not automatically yield an event's full meaning. Respect for different sources of knowledge does not require giving them equal weight on every question. Different materials may each supply content that cannot be substituted for the others.

2.6.1Note

Understanding this section

2.6.1 Analogy, Formal Instances, and Tested Comparisons

Resembling something, belonging to the same class within a model, and being supported in the target world are three different statuses. Keeping them separate neither devalues analogy nor lends it evidential force it has not acquired.

The first is heuristic analogy: explain similarities and differences and propose a relation worth testing. The second is a formal instance: variables and operations satisfy all premises of a mathematical proposition, so the conclusion follows by proof within that model, irrespective of whether the stories seem alike. The third is a tested target-domain relation: independent materials together with bridges support the specific relation, and the support comes from those materials, not from calling it similar. The three can work together in one study, but must not automatically be upgraded from one status to another.

For example, the existence of a path in an abstract graph is a formal property. Mapping an actual link to the ability to send information requires checking that the corresponding channel is available. Claiming that information actually traveled through it and changed an outcome requires further evidence of events and effects. Even with isomorphic graphs, edges representing cooperation, power supply, or kinship have entirely different meanings for real-world operations.

Historical and archaeological materials require even clearer separation of layers: how traces physically formed is one layer; which activity or function they correspond to is another; the social relations and institutions involving participants are a third. Similar tool marks may raise questions about activities, but do not automatically identify the same power regime. Kinship identification can support a biological relationship without by itself showing who ruled whom. More accurate dating helps establish sequence, but does not by itself answer what an event meant.

Respecting different sources of knowledge does not mean giving them equal weight for every question. Dating measurements, genetic relations, local knowledge, oral accounts, and textual context may each answer non-interchangeable questions. Material unsuited to one claim is not thereby useless for every question. Conversely, the importance of a form of knowledge must not exempt it from criticism required for the proposed use.

This section continues using the ancient-DNA study but adds a new focus: the scope of support for identifying a relation. Kinship conclusions depend on genetic materials and interpretation, whereas conclusions about rule or normative standing need separate social evidence. This limit is the lesson's analysis of how the material may be used; it does not invent political conclusions that the study's authors never proposed and then refute them.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Classification premise: specify whether the item is a proposal of similarity, an instance of mathematical premises, or an empirical comparison supported by target-domain materials.

  2. 2

    Formal connection: if graph isomorphism or an instance of a proposition is claimed, verify one by one the objects, relations, and operations preserved by the mapping. Only preserved properties may transfer through the proof.

  3. 3

    Empirical connection: real-world relations require examination of material generation, operations, timing, identities, and alternative explanations. Formal isomorphism does not directly establish actual use or causal effects.

  4. 4

    Historical connection: moving from traces to functions and then to social relations requires listing new assumptions and discriminating materials at each step. Evidence at other layers must not manufacture truth for a missing layer.

  5. 5

    Conclusion: tested comparison may enter an argument, but must precisely identify where support comes from and retain relations that have not been tested as such.

Distinctions to keep clear

Formal instance

The object and mapping satisfy specified mathematical premises.

≠

Evidence for a real-world instance

The target-domain mapping and premises have appropriate observational and design support.

Genetic kinship

An evidential judgment about biological relatedness.

≠

Social power

Roles, rules, domination, resources, and institutional relations; these must not be inferred automatically from kinship.

Similar traces

Clues to possible formation processes.

≠

The same institution

Requires additional grounds concerning activities and social relations.

Teaching mathematical construction: isomorphic graphs can transfer reachability, not powerTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth graphs and all edges are stipulated for teaching. Authorization chain/contact among colleagues are merely two hypothetical interpretations.

Let G₁ have nodes {a,b,c} and edges {a→b,b→c}, and G₂ have nodes {1,2,3} and edges {1→2,2→3}. The mapping a↦1, b↦2, c↦3 preserves each edge, so if a path exists from a to c in G₁, a path exists from 1 to 3 in G₂. If one graph is interpreted as an authorization chain and the other as contact among colleagues, graph isomorphism does not also prove the authorization semantics.

BoundaryThe proof covers only reachability in the graphs. It does not establish that the actual relations exist, that information is transmitted, or who has authority to act.

The father–daughter relationship at Chagyrskaya: which relation do the materials support?Documented case

In Genetic relationships, Skov et al.'s 2022 paper combines first-degree relatedness with different mitochondrial genomes to identify Chagyrskaya H as D's daughter. This lesson distinguishes the scope of that finding: it is a kinship judgment supported by genetic materials. Ruling status or institutions must not be added solely on the basis of that relation.

SourceSkov et al. 2022, main-text kinship analysisNature 610 (2022), 519–525; the paragraph beginning “One adult male individual, Chagyrskaya D” in Genetic relationships in the PMC text, and Table 1Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe statement that kinship does not automatically establish rule is this lesson's limitation on use. It does not claim that the paper's authors proposed or rejected a particular ruling system, or generalize from this site to all Neanderthal societies.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: tools from two burials show very similar wear, and a researcher directly concludes that the two places had the same ruling institutions.

What it limitsThis skips at least the several bridges between trace formation, activity functions, and social relations. Return to candidate status and examine the relevant materials.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Unresolved boundaryKinship evidence can support a father–daughter relationship, but by itself cannot distinguish multiple possible arrangements of social power.

What it limitsLeave power relations unresolved rather than withdrawing the grounded kinship result.

Skov et al. 2022, kinship analysis (the same study)

What does not follow

  • The father–daughter conclusion in the ancient-DNA study does not by itself establish male rule, inheritance rules, or the community's full institutional arrangements. This lesson does not claim that such institutions were necessarily absent; this material is simply insufficient to decide.
  • Formal isomorphism preserves the registered structural properties, not every everyday meaning and causal parameter. More accurate dating likewise does not automatically recover an event's entire meaning.
  • Comparative research need not always be merely suggestive. After testing with independent target-domain materials, it may take on limited argumentative responsibilities according to its actual design.

Scope and open questions

This actual study clearly illustrates the kind of relation supported by materials and the additional responsibilities of social interpretation. It reuses the preceding section's case without repeating its analogy narrative.

  • Questions about rule, rights, and institutions require additional materials on activities, resources, and social relations. This lesson has not obtained evidence capable of deciding these questions.

No. Isomorphism preserves only the relational structure defined in the graph. Actual edge meanings, processes, resources, operations, and outcomes require separate examination.

Does identifying two ancient individuals as father and daughter directly justify writing that the father ruled the community?

No. Kinship and rule are different relations; the latter requires social and institutional evidence. Uncertainty about rule does not cancel the kinship evidence.

After an analogy gains independent target-domain materials, does its support come from the analogy itself?

2.7Source Protocol ​

In briefA source list is not better merely because it is longer. Each judgment should lead back to the precise location that supports it. Citing theory to explain how to test something does not mean that real-world test results have been obtained.

Source records must specify the source domain, case type, time and region, scope of support, and limits of extrapolation item by item, and complete counterexample registration. Original materials, secondary interpretations, and this framework's inferences are kept in separate columns. Judgments in the text and their original locations are linked in both directions, so that readers can return from a judgment to the materials and see from the materials which limited claim they have been used to support.

Conceptual definitions, field mappings, and method descriptions specify only what is to be tested, how it is to be recorded, and where to stop drawing conclusions. They must not enter empirical_evidence_records as object facts or mechanism support. Internal terms, identifiers, examples, and the framework's own formulations cannot replace external materials. In other words, a method definition is not the same as empirical support.

Empirical support must come from independently registered instance materials and include the object and scale, time window, research design, N0, outcomes, uncertainty, review or reproduction, and evidential level. Without corresponding external instance materials, specific empirical assertions within the G question families cannot acquire formal empirical support. C is used separately for outcome registration, mechanism conditions, and normative bridging; real-world mechanism judgments under CM still need the corresponding instance evidence. A question catalog, outcome contracts, and the framework's own descriptions cannot replace the missing materials.

2.7Note

Understanding this section

2.7 Source Protocol

A source list is not better merely because it is longer. Each judgment should lead back to the precise location that supports it. Citing theory to explain how to test something does not mean that real-world test results have been obtained.

For each source, record the domain, case type, time and region, scope of support, limits of extrapolation, and relevant counterexamples. Separate original materials, secondary interpretations, and inferences made within this framework, so readers can trace a judgment to its original location and see which limited claims a given material is being used to support. Bidirectional links serve to check whether inference exceeds its bounds, not to label sources as authoritative.

Concept definitions, field mappings, and method explanations determine what to ask, how to record it, and where to stop. They must not enter empirical_evidence_records as object facts or support for mechanisms. For example, the book's definition of how G2 tests a specified channel does not establish that the channel exists in an actual object. Its account of how C combines results does not mean that actual materials already support every combined link.

Applications for formal empirical support require separately registered instance materials: object and scale, time window, research design, N0, results, uncertainty, review or replication, and evidential level. This follows the two-stage admission in §2.1; it does not force every archive into a modern experimental format. Ordinary domain evidence retains its original design, while formal G support is obtained under the corresponding contract.

C serves different purposes, including registering results, specifying mechanism conditions, and normative bridging. It must not uniformly be treated as additional causal facts. CM judgments about actual mechanisms still require corresponding instance evidence. Question catalogues, outcome contracts, and explanations of the framework itself can at most specify testing responsibilities. Repeated citation will not fill gaps in external materials.

Sources closer to the original generation of information generally make specific details easier to check, but original materials may also contain errors, omissions, or interpretation. Examine version, generation process, precise location, and correspondence to claims separately; primary must not mean beyond criticism. The next section addresses source relations and reading scope, and the following section addresses independence and how errors propagate.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: a document may contain definitions, facts, the author's interpretations, and unresolved speculation; different passages support different objects of inquiry.

  2. 2

    Connection: register each claim's source location and support ceiling, separating original material, others' interpretations, and this lesson's inferences, so that the appropriateness of borrowing can be checked.

  3. 3

    Exclusion: a method contract alone contains no instance results. It must not be inserted into empirical records to support the existence of a mechanism.

  4. 4

    Conclusion: strong claims concerning formal G/CM support require corresponding external instance materials. Existing domain materials retain their actual design; numbers or citation counts must not upgrade them.

  5. 5

    Review responsibility: when a claim changes, recheck the support relation. The same document may support a date fact without supporting a net causal narrative beginning on that date.

Distinctions to keep clear

Method source

Provides terms, design, or recording rules.

≠

Empirical source

Provides objects, observations, or instance results whose scope of support must be assessed.

Primary record

Close to the actual generation process, with specific locations that can be checked.

≠

Unconditional truth

No source has this privilege; original records still have limitations.

Source support

Specifically supports a bounded claim.

≠

Authoritative endorsement

Using prestige to bypass the support relation cannot substitute for evidence.

Teaching construction: two usable kinds of content in one manualTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe manual, threshold, and actual measurement are all teaching assumptions; no real publication is identified.

Suppose a manual's first chapter defines an acceptable reading as having error no greater than e, while an appendix records the error in one actual measurement. The definition supports the term's meaning, not the acceptability of that measurement. Only if measurement and calculation are reliable might the appendix data support the instance judgment. If the appendix is merely a worked example, it still cannot become a real-world measurement.

BoundaryThe example illustrates source roles; it does not certify any actual equipment or instance.

One original work, different scopes of support for different sentencesDocumented case

Pages 51–52 also limit an interpretation attributing the subsequent decline directly to that action. This section links these locations separately to event dates and limits on causal attribution.

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceSnow recounts the September 7 interview and removal of the handle the following day, while later retaining the qualification that the decline had begun before the pump was disabled.

What it limitsThe same source supports the event date, but the existence of that date does not justify jumping to the claim that removing the handle caused the entire decline.

What does not follow

  • Neither the source text nor the skill can independently certify its empirical assertions about the real world. This lesson cites the theory only to explain what the author says and under which conditions.
  • Numerous references and complete bibliographic information only make checking easier; they do not replace the support relation between claims and facts.
  • Existing historical evidence need not be discarded because it has not become a G-instance, but its historical standing does not automatically confer formal G eligibility either.

Scope and open questions

Two passages in the same original work can support judgments of different scope, directly demonstrating claim-by-claim source registration.
